---
title: "Empty Stadiums and the Crowd Channel in Home-Field Advantage"
subtitle: "A four-league natural experiment and what it cannot resolve"
author: "Jayden Gould"
date: today
abstract: |
  Home teams win more often than away teams in every major North American sport, taking between
  52.8% and 57.0% of decided regular-season games in full-crowd seasons, but the share
  of that advantage attributable to the crowd itself is hard to separate from
  travel, familiarity, scheduling and officiating. The 2020–21 COVID-19 attendance restrictions
  offer a natural experiment: for one season in the NFL, NBA and NHL and two in MLB, professional
  games were played in empty or capacity-capped buildings. We assemble a unified game-level panel of
  30,146 games across the NFL, MLB, NBA and NHL (seasons 2018–2023) with per-game crowd dose measured
  as announced attendance over an empirical venue-season capacity, and estimate the crowd-attributable
  slice of home advantage with two co-primary estimators: a team fixed-effects dose-response
  regression, and a comparative interrupted time series in which the away team serves as the
  implicit control group. Point estimates on home win probability are +0.050 (NFL), +0.006 (NBA),
  +0.011 (NHL) and −0.021 (MLB); every per-sport interval crosses zero. **The finding of this paper
  is not that null. It is a ceiling.** In all eight sport × outcome cells, per unit of crowd dose,
  the effect this design could detect at 80% power exceeds that sport's entire home-field advantage,
  the smallest (NBA win probability) by 6%. Rescaled to each league's normal-season crowd dose, three
  cells fall to approximately one or below. The constraint is that the treatment was assigned to
  seasons, not games: each league has one restricted season (MLB has two), and in every cell at least
  one ordinary season deviated further from trend than the restricted season did. On that
  season-level basis, a decomposition of season-to-season variance shows that extending the panel
  would leave the detectable effect above the whole home advantage in seven of eight cells. Where a
  published causal estimate can be mapped into our units (the NBA), it sits at the upper edge of our
  NBA margin interval. Randomization inference over the five or six season-level treatment assignments each
  league actually has cannot reject any hypothesis below p = 0.167, zero and a full-advantage effect
  alike. The team-clustered intervals do exclude a full-advantage effect in two cells (MLB and NBA win
  probability). For the NBA, season-level noise that those intervals ignore puts the detectable
  effect back above the whole advantage. MLB win probability is the one cell where the data lean
  against a crowd effect that large. It rests on the assumption that nothing else home-specific
  changed in 2020–21, which baseball's 2020 rule changes make least safe, and on 2021 crowd doses
  that overlap heavily with normal seasons. We set out precisely why this design has the ceiling it
  has.
format:

    toc: true
    toc-depth: 3

```{python}
#| label: setup
import sys, pathlib, numpy as np, pandas as pd
from IPython.display import Markdown

ROOT = pathlib.Path.cwd()
while not (ROOT / "results" / "tables").exists() and ROOT != ROOT.parent:
    ROOT = ROOT.parent
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))
T = ROOT / "results" / "tables"
FIG = ROOT / "results" / "figures"

def csv(name):
    return pd.read_csv(T / f"{name}.csv")

def md(df, index=False):
    """Minimal markdown table (avoids a tabulate dependency)."""
    d = df.reset_index() if index else df
    cols = [str(c) for c in d.columns]
    lines = ["| " + " | ".join(cols) + " |",
             "|" + "|".join("---" for _ in cols) + "|"]
    for _, r in d.iterrows():
        lines.append("| " + " | ".join("" if pd.isna(v) else str(v) for v in r) + " |")
    return Markdown("\n".join(lines))

SPORTS = ["nfl", "mlb", "nba", "nhl"]
UP = {"nfl": "NFL", "mlb": "MLB", "nba": "NBA", "nhl": "NHL"}
def ci(lo, hi, d=3):
    return f"[{lo:+.{d}f}, {hi:+.{d}f}]"

import yaml
TREATED = {s: v["treated_seasons"] for s, v in
           yaml.safe_load((ROOT / "config" / "sports.yaml").read_text()).items()
           if isinstance(v, dict) and "treated_seasons" in v}
_MINUS = "−"
def num(v, d=3):   return f"{v:.{d}f}".replace("-", _MINUS)
def sgn(v, d=3):   return f"{v:+.{d}f}".replace("-", _MINUS)
def pct(v, d=1):   return f"{v * 100:.{d}f}%".replace("-", _MINUS)
def pp(v, d=1):    return f"{v * 100:.{d}f}".replace("-", _MINUS)
def thou(n):       return f"{int(round(n)):,}"
def dot(v, d=3):   # .639 style; only strips a leading zero ("10.593" stays "10.593")
    s = num(v, d)
    return s[1:] if s.startswith("0.") else s.replace(_MINUS + "0.", _MINUS + ".")
def times(v, d=2): return f"{v:.{d}f}×"
def civ(lo, hi, d=3):
    """Bracketed [lo, hi] CI using sgn() so both bounds get the Unicode minus
    the draft uses (ci() above is table-only and keeps an ASCII hyphen)."""
    return f"[{sgn(lo, d)}, {sgn(hi, d)}]"
_W = ("zero one two three four five six seven eight nine ten eleven twelve thirteen fourteen "
      "fifteen sixteen seventeen eighteen nineteen twenty twenty-one twenty-two").split()
def words(n):      return _W[int(n)]
assert (sgn(-0.0193), sgn(0.046), pct(0.528), thou(30169), dot(0.639), dot(10.593), words(7), times(1.018), pct(-0.05), pp(-0.0193), words(22), civ(-1.002, 4.297, 1)) == \
       ("−0.019", "+0.046", "52.8%", "30,169", ".639", "10.593", "seven", "1.02×", "−5.0%", "−1.9", "twenty-two", "[−1.0, +4.3]")

desc = csv("descriptive_hfa")
twfe_all = pd.concat([csv(f"twfe_{s}") for s in SPORTS])
did_all = pd.concat([csv(f"did_{s}") for s in SPORTS])
meta = csv("meta_cross_sport")
noise = csv("noise_floor")
seasonfx = csv("season_effects")
loso = csv("leave_one_season_out")
overlap = csv("dose_overlap")
trend = csv("trend_sensitivity")
sfe = csv("season_fe_sensitivity")
within = csv("within_season_dose")
travel = csv("twfe_nhl_travel_diagnostic")
mlbsplit = csv("mlb_treated_split")
zsens = csv("zero_attendance_sensitivity")
rsens = csv("reopen_zero_sensitivity")

def pick(df, **kw):
    m = np.ones(len(df), bool)
    for k, v in kw.items():
        m &= (df[k] == v).values
    return df[m].iloc[0]
```

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

```{python}
#| label: intro-vars
#| include: false
assert [len(TREATED[s]) for s in ("nfl", "nba", "nhl", "mlb")] == [1, 1, 1, 2]
def _season_label(y):
    """A season ending in year y, in the paper's own 'the 2020–21 NHL season' convention."""
    return f"{y - 1}–{y % 100:02d}"

_load = yaml.safe_load((ROOT / "config" / "sports.yaml").read_text())["nfl"]["load_seasons"]
intro_n_seasons = _load[1] - _load[0] + 1

_fc = desc[desc["season"] == "pooled_fullcrowd"]
intro_hfa_win_min = _fc["home_win_pct"].min()
intro_hfa_win_max = _fc["home_win_pct"].max()

_intro_hfa = {s: {"home_margin": pick(desc, sport=s, season="pooled_fullcrowd")["mean_home_margin"],
                   "home_win": pick(desc, sport=s, season="pooled_fullcrowd")["home_win_pct"] - 0.5}
              for s in SPORTS}
_LAB = {"home_margin": "margin", "home_win": "win probability"}

intro_mde_gt1_count = sum(
    (2.8 * pick(twfe_all, sport=s, outcome=oc, sample="pooled")["se"]) / _intro_hfa[s][oc] > 1
    for s in SPORTS for oc in ("home_margin", "home_win")
)
assert intro_mde_gt1_count == len(SPORTS) * 2
_intro_ratios = {(s, oc): (2.8 * pick(twfe_all, sport=s, outcome=oc, sample="pooled")["se"]) / _intro_hfa[s][oc]
                  for s in SPORTS for oc in ("home_margin", "home_win")}
intro_mde_min_ratio = min(_intro_ratios.values())
_min_ratio_cell = min(_intro_ratios, key=_intro_ratios.get)
intro_min_ratio_label = f"{UP[_min_ratio_cell[0]]} {_LAB[_min_ratio_cell[1]]}"

import math
def _phi(x):
    return 0.5 * (1 + math.erf(x / 2 ** 0.5))
def _power(s, oc):
    se = pick(twfe_all, sport=s, outcome=oc, sample="pooled")["se"]
    hfa = _intro_hfa[s][oc]
    return _phi(hfa / se - 1.96) + _phi(-hfa / se - 1.96)
intro_power_lt_half_count = sum(_power(s, oc) < 0.5 for s in SPORTS for oc in ("home_margin", "home_win"))
# the same count against the full-advantage effect rescaled to each league's control dose.
def _power_rescaled(s, oc):
    se = pick(twfe_all, sport=s, outcome=oc, sample="pooled")["se"]
    hfa = _intro_hfa[s][oc] / pick(overlap, sport=s, scope="all_treated")["control_mean"]
    return _phi(hfa / se - 1.96) + _phi(-hfa / se - 1.96)
intro_power_lt_half_rescaled_count = sum(_power_rescaled(s, oc) < 0.5 for s in SPORTS for oc in ("home_margin", "home_win"))

_excl_cells = []
for s in SPORTS:
    for oc in ("home_margin", "home_win"):
        _row = pick(twfe_all, sport=s, outcome=oc, sample="pooled")
        _cm = pick(overlap, sport=s, scope="all_treated")["control_mean"]
        _hfa = _intro_hfa[s][oc]
        _excl_unit = _row["ci_high"] < _hfa or _row["ci_low"] > _hfa
        _excl_rescaled = _row["ci_high"] < _hfa / _cm or _row["ci_low"] > _hfa / _cm
        if _excl_unit and _excl_rescaled:
            _excl_cells.append((s, oc))
intro_excl_count = len(_excl_cells)
intro_excl_cells_str = ", ".join(f"{UP[s]} {_LAB[oc]}" for s, oc in _excl_cells)
# pin the abstract's typed "two cells (MLB and NBA win probability)" to
# this live set, so the next data change fails loudly here instead of only going stale silently.
assert set(_excl_cells) == {("mlb", "home_win"), ("nba", "home_win")}, \
    "full-advantage exclusion set no longer matches the abstract's typed 'two cells' claim; reword the abstract"

intro_floor_count = int((noise["ratio_floor"] >= 1).sum())
# the abstract/intro/conclusion say the NBA win exclusion fails against the season-level floor,
# MLB win is the one cell below it, and (abstract) every cell has an untreated season deviating further
# than the treated one. Break loudly if the data stop saying so.
_nf = noise.set_index(["sport", "outcome"])["ratio_floor"]
assert _nf[("nba", "home_win")] > 1 and _nf[("mlb", "home_win")] < 1 and intro_floor_count == 7, \
    "reword the NBA/MLB exclusion sentences (abstract, intro, conclusion)"
assert all(g.loc[~g["is_treated"], "coef"].abs().max() > g.loc[g["is_treated"], "coef"].abs().max()
           for _, g in seasonfx.groupby(["sport", "outcome"])), "reword the abstract's 'in every cell at least one ordinary season'"

intro_nfl_win_coef = pick(twfe_all, sport="nfl", outcome="home_win", sample="pooled")["coef"]
intro_nfl_win_loso = pick(loso, sport="nfl", outcome="home_win", dropped_season=2018)["coef"]
```

Home teams tend to win. Across the four major North American professional leagues, in the
full-crowd seasons of the `{python} words(intro_n_seasons)` seasons studied here, the home side takes
between `{python} pct(intro_hfa_win_min)` and `{python} pct(intro_hfa_win_max)` of decided
regular-season games. The existence of home-field advantage is one of the most dependable patterns
in sport. Its *causes* are not.

The candidate mechanisms are well rehearsed and badly identified. Home teams do not travel to
the game, while away teams do. Home teams know the sightlines, the ice, the wind, the mound. Home
teams bat last, or get the last line change. On top of that, home teams play in front of a partisan
crowd, whose noise is widely believed to intimidate visitors, to drown out the visiting offense's
snap count, and to bend the marginal officiating decision.
These channels move together in ordinary data: the team that has the crowd is the same team that
skipped the flight and knows the building.

The attendance restrictions of 2020–21 disrupted the crowd channel far more than any other. They
covered the NFL's `{python} TREATED["nfl"][0]` season, the NBA's
`{python} _season_label(TREATED["nba"][0])` and the NHL's `{python} _season_label(TREATED["nhl"][0])`
seasons, and MLB's `{python} TREATED["mlb"][0]` and `{python} TREATED["mlb"][1]` seasons.
Familiarity, the rulebook's home-team privileges and the schedule's home-and-away structure
largely persisted. Not everything else held still, though: schedules, rosters, travel and, in
baseball, the rules changed too (@sec-assumption states what that does to the estimate). If the
crowd is worth a measurable share of home advantage, that share should have gone missing.

This paper does two things. First, it **quantifies** home-field advantage descriptively across
four leagues on a common panel, in both win percentage and scoring margin. Second, it estimates
the **crowd-attributable slice** of that advantage, using the attendance restrictions as the
source of variation in crowd size, with the sport treated throughout as a parameter. We have one schema, one feature pipeline, two estimators and four leagues.

Every per-league interval crosses zero. The largest point estimate, the NFL's
`{python} sgn(intro_nfl_win_coef)` on win probability, falls to `{python} sgn(intro_nfl_win_loso)`
when the 2018 season is dropped (@sec-loso). We want to be careful about what that means, because a
common way this literature is misread is to treat an imprecise estimate as an informative one. Our
central claim is therefore about resolution rather than magnitude:

> In all `{python} words(intro_mde_gt1_count)` sport × outcome cells, per unit of crowd dose, the
> effect this design could detect at 80% power exceeds that sport's entire home-field advantage,
> the smallest (`{python} intro_min_ratio_label`) by `{python} pct(intro_mde_min_ratio - 1, 0)`. At
> per-unit scaling, a crowd effect equal to the whole home advantage would more likely than not go
> undetected in `{python} words(intro_power_lt_half_count)` of eight cells; rescaled to each league's
> normal-season dose, in `{python} words(intro_power_lt_half_rescaled_count)`.

This is not a hedge appended to a null result. It is the result.
`{python} words(intro_excl_count).capitalize()` of these cells' team-clustered intervals
(`{python} intro_excl_cells_str`) exclude a full-advantage effect. The NBA's does not hold against
the season-level noise floor (@sec-floor). MLB win probability is the one cell where the data lean
against a crowd effect as large as the whole advantage, on an assumption that baseball's 2020 rule
changes make least safe (@sec-mlb). The rest of the paper is an
attempt to say exactly how large the effect would have to be before we could see it, why the design
has that ceiling, whether anything could raise it, and where our intervals sit relative to the
published literature. Adding seasons would not raise the ceiling: on the season-level basis (not
per unit of crowd dose), the smallest effect detectable against the design's irreducible noise
floor exceeds the entire home advantage in `{python} words(intro_floor_count)` of eight cells
(@sec-floor). Section [-@sec-lit] shows that, in the one league where a published causal estimate
can be mapped into our units, that estimate sits at the upper edge of our interval. This is a statement about our precision,
not a corroboration of their finding. Our point estimate is about a third of it.

**This study was not pre-registered.** It was built under an internal pre-commitment discipline,
with one exception we disclose here. The primary specification was first written with full season
fixed effects. Its first real-data run returned all twelve crowd coefficients negative (three
leagues, two outcomes and two samples at the time), which we traced to season dummies being near-collinear with a season-level
treatment, and we changed the model once, to team fixed effects and a linear trend (@sec-notwfe;
@tbl-sfe reports the original structure for every cell). It has not been re-specified since, and
the NHL was added afterward under that frozen specification. Diagnostics were reported whichever
way they came out. Internal discipline is not a public
timestamp, though, and we do not claim the credibility of one. Complete disclosure is the
substitute we can offer, and Sections [-@sec-robust] and [-@sec-limits] are written to that
standard.

# Data {#sec-data}

```{python}
#| label: data-vars
#| include: false
from src.features.build import elo_accuracy

_sports_cfg = yaml.safe_load((ROOT / "config" / "sports.yaml").read_text())

def _elo_acc(sport):
    panel = pd.read_parquet(ROOT / "data" / "processed" / f"{sport}.parquet",
                             columns=["home_elo", "away_elo", "home_margin"])
    acc, _ = elo_accuracy(panel, _sports_cfg[sport]["elo"]["hfa"])
    return acc

data_n_schema_cols = len(pd.read_parquet(ROOT / "data" / "processed" / "nfl.parquet").columns)

data_elo_acc_nfl = _elo_acc("nfl")
data_elo_acc_mlb = _elo_acc("mlb")
data_elo_acc_nba = _elo_acc("nba")
data_elo_acc_nhl = _elo_acc("nhl")

data_dose_ctrl_nfl = pick(overlap, sport="nfl", scope="all_treated")["control_mean"]
data_dose_ctrl_nba = pick(overlap, sport="nba", scope="all_treated")["control_mean"]
data_dose_ctrl_nhl = pick(overlap, sport="nhl", scope="all_treated")["control_mean"]
data_dose_ctrl_mlb = pick(overlap, sport="mlb", scope="all_treated")["control_mean"]

data_n_leagues_low_overlap = sum(
    1 for s in SPORTS
    if pick(overlap, sport=s, scope="all_treated")["control_overlap"] < 0.006
)

data_mlb_overlap_pooled = pick(overlap, sport="mlb", scope="all_treated")["control_overlap"]
data_mlb_overlap_2020 = pick(overlap, sport="mlb", scope="2020")["control_overlap"]
data_mlb_overlap_2021 = pick(overlap, sport="mlb", scope="2021")["control_overlap"]
data_mlb_treated_mean_2021 = pick(overlap, sport="mlb", scope="2021")["treated_mean"]
data_nfl_overlap = pick(overlap, sport="nfl", scope="all_treated")["control_overlap"]
assert data_mlb_overlap_2020 <= data_nfl_overlap, "MLB 2020 overlap now exceeds the NFL's; reword 'no more than'"

# Zero-attendance correction (spec 2026-09-15): games whose ESPN attendance is 0 outside every
# restriction window carry null crowd_pct in data/processed.
data_zero_nulled = {s: int(pick(zsens, sport=s, outcome="home_win")["n_nulled"]) for s in SPORTS}
data_zero_nulled_total = sum(data_zero_nulled.values())
_mlb_z = pd.read_parquet(ROOT / "data" / "processed" / "mlb.parquet",
                         columns=["date", "home_team", "attendance", "crowd_pct"])
# Doubleheader = another game by the same home team within 12 hours. `date` is UTC, so a
# calendar-day grouping would split evening doubleheaders across midnight.
_mlb_z = _mlb_z.sort_values("date")
_gap = _mlb_z.groupby("home_team")["date"].diff()
_gap_next = _mlb_z.groupby("home_team")["date"].diff(-1).abs()
_mlb_z_dh = (_gap <= pd.Timedelta("12h")) | (_gap_next <= pd.Timedelta("12h"))
data_zero_mlb_dh = int(((_mlb_z["attendance"] == 0) & _mlb_z["crowd_pct"].isna() & _mlb_z_dh).sum())
assert _sports_cfg["mlb"]["zero_attendance_windows"] == [{"seasons": TREATED["mlb"][:1]}], \
    "MLB zero-attendance window no longer 'first treated season only'; reword the window sentence"
assert data_zero_mlb_dh > data_zero_nulled["mlb"] / 2, "most MLB nulled zeros are no longer doubleheaders; reword"

# Reopening rule (spec 2026-09-16): treated-season zeros after a team's first game with fans.
data_reopen_nulled = {s: int(pick(rsens, sport=s, outcome="home_win")["n_nulled"]) for s in SPORTS}
data_reopen_nulled_total = sum(data_reopen_nulled.values())

# split those nulls into "team has a sourced fans_from
# entry" vs. "date is the data's own first non-zero attendance alone, for a team with none".
# Re-derives src.features.build.null_reporting_zeros's own `real`/`reopened` booleans straight
# from `attendance` (never nulled) and config, so it needs no gitignored audit file and cannot
# drift from the actual rule that built these tables.
def _reopen_split(sport):
    df = pd.read_parquet(ROOT / "data" / "processed" / f"{sport}.parquet")
    day = pd.to_datetime(df["date"]).dt.normalize()
    cs = _sports_cfg[sport]
    real = pd.Series(False, index=df.index)
    for w in cs["zero_attendance_windows"]:
        m = pd.Series(True, index=df.index)
        if "seasons" in w:
            m &= df["season"].isin(w["seasons"])
        if "start" in w:
            m &= (day >= pd.Timestamp(w["start"])) & (day <= pd.Timestamp(w["end"]))
        if "home_teams" in w:
            m &= df["home_team"].isin(w["home_teams"])
        real |= m
    audited = (df["season"].isin(cs["treated_seasons"]) & ~df["is_playoff"] & ~df["is_bubble"]
               & ~df["neutral_site"] & ~df["relocated_home"])
    first = day.where(audited & (df["attendance"] > 0)).groupby([df["season"], df["home_team"]]).transform("min")
    sourced_mask = pd.Series(False, index=df.index)
    for f in cs["fans_from"]:
        d = pd.Timestamp(f["date"])
        m = (df["season"] == f["season"]) & (df["home_team"] == f["team"])
        first = first.where(~m | (first <= d), d)
        sourced_mask |= m
    reopened = audited & (day >= first)
    for r in cs["reclosures"]:
        reopened &= ~((df["home_team"] == r["team"]) & (day >= pd.Timestamp(r["start"]))
                      & (day <= pd.Timestamp(r["end"])))
    newly = (df["attendance"] == 0) & real & reopened   # real under fix 1, flipped by this rule
    return df, newly, sourced_mask

_reopen_detail = {s: _reopen_split(s) for s in SPORTS}
data_reopen_sourced_null = sum(int((newly & sm).sum()) for _, newly, sm in _reopen_detail.values())
data_reopen_unsourced_null = sum(int((newly & ~sm).sum()) for _, newly, sm in _reopen_detail.values())
assert data_reopen_sourced_null + data_reopen_unsourced_null == data_reopen_nulled_total, \
    "reopening-null sourced/unsourced split no longer sums to the total; reword the Data-section sentence"

_nhl_df, _nhl_newly, _nhl_sourced_mask = _reopen_detail["nhl"]
_nhl_audited = (_nhl_df["season"].isin(_sports_cfg["nhl"]["treated_seasons"]) & ~_nhl_df["is_playoff"]
                & ~_nhl_df["is_bubble"] & ~_nhl_df["neutral_site"] & ~_nhl_df["relocated_home"])
data_reopen_nsh_stl_n = {t: int((_nhl_audited & (_nhl_df["home_team"] == t)).sum()) for t in ("NSH", "STL")}
assert (data_reopen_nsh_stl_n["NSH"] == data_reopen_nsh_stl_n["STL"]
        and all(int((_nhl_audited & (_nhl_df["home_team"] == t) & (_nhl_df["attendance"] > 0)).sum()) == 0
                for t in ("NSH", "STL"))), \
    "Nashville/St. Louis no longer both all-zero all season; reword the Data-section NSH/STL sentence"

data_untreated_before_nfl = TREATED["nfl"][0] - _sports_cfg["nfl"]["load_seasons"][0]
data_untreated_before_nba = TREATED["nba"][0] - _sports_cfg["nba"]["load_seasons"][0]
assert (TREATED["mlb"][0] - _sports_cfg["mlb"]["load_seasons"][0] == data_untreated_before_nfl
        and TREATED["nhl"][0] - _sports_cfg["nhl"]["load_seasons"][0] == data_untreated_before_nba), \
    "NFL/MLB and NBA/NHL no longer share an untreated-season count; reword the load-window sentence"
```

## Sources

All four leagues are sourced from ESPN's public site API [@espn_data] and keyed on the ESPN event
identifier, so the pipeline carries no cross-source join apart from the one id-keyed NFL join
described below. Two endpoints are used: the
daily *scoreboard* (event id, teams, final scores, venue, neutral-site flag, status) and the
per-game *summary* (announced attendance). The NFL is a partial exception. Its schedule, closing
betting spread, rest days, weather, roof type and referee come from `nfl_data_py`, joined to ESPN
attendance on the schedule's ESPN id column.

Sport-native packages were spiked first and rejected, each for the same reason in a different
form: attendance is either absent (`nba_api` returns `None`; `nfl_data_py` carries no attendance
at all), blocked (Pro-Football-Reference 403s automated requests), or, worst of all,
systematically missing for exactly the games this study depends on (`pybaseball` inherits
Baseball-Reference's "Unknown" attendance for 2020 empty games, which arrives as `NaN` rather
than zero, nulling the treatment).

The load window is seasons 2018–2023 for every league: `{python} words(data_untreated_before_nfl)` untreated seasons before the
restriction window for the NFL and MLB, `{python} words(data_untreated_before_nba)` for the NBA and NHL, and two or three after. That
window lets a linear time trend be separated from the treated season, and lets the empirical
capacity definition below anchor itself.

## Panel

Every league normalizes into one game-level schema of `{python} data_n_schema_cols` columns, one row per game, identical
across sports; leagues null what does not apply to them (MLB has no point spread, indoor sports
have no weather). All sport-specific handling lives in the loaders. Everything downstream
(features, models, figures) is sport-blind.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-panel
#| tbl-cap: "Panel sizes. The estimation sample is smaller than the loaded panel because of the exclusions in @sec-exclusions and listwise deletion on controls (chiefly rest days, undefined for a team's first game of a season)."
#| output: asis
panel_rows = []
for s in SPORTS:
    n_loaded = len(pd.read_parquet(ROOT / "data" / "processed" / f"{s}.parquet", columns=["sport"]))
    n_est = int(pick(twfe_all, sport=s, outcome="home_margin", sample="pooled")["n_obs"])
    panel_rows.append({
        "League": UP[s],
        "Games loaded": thou(n_loaded),
        "Estimation sample (margin)": thou(n_est),
        "Treated season(s)": ", ".join(str(y) for y in TREATED[s]),
    })
display(md(pd.DataFrame(panel_rows)))
```

Treated seasons differ by league and are configuration, never a hardcoded year. The NFL played its
2020 season under restrictions; MLB's 2020 season was entirely empty and its 2021 season partially
capped; the NBA and NHL restrictions fall in their 2021 seasons (NBA and NHL seasons are labeled by the
calendar year in which they end, so 2021 = 2020–21). An earlier version of the
data-sanity gate hardcoded 2020 and returned a false PASS for the NBA off a coincidental gap; the
gate is now driven entirely by the configured treatment labels.

## Crowd dose {#sec-dose}

The treatment variable is `crowd_pct`, announced attendance divided by an **empirical** capacity,
defined as the maximum announced attendance that venue recorded in that season. This is not the
seated capacity of the building, and the difference is material. ESPN's own `venue.capacity`
field is always null, and announced attendance (tickets distributed) routinely exceeds seated
capacity: roughly 60% of NFL games, with Dallas announcing ~93,000 in an 80,000-seat stadium.
No public turnstile series exists, and an empirical, self-calibrating denominator is the only
definition available that keeps the ratio interpretable.

Treated venue-seasons *borrow* the venue's untreated maximum (taking the larger of the borrowed
value and their own), so a capped season cannot define its own full house. Which seasons borrow is
decided from the configured treatment labels, never from a magnitude threshold. A magnitude rule
misfires on the partial 2021 reopenings, where a genuinely full house can follow a capped one
within the same season.

Two properties of this variable matter for everything that follows:

1. **`crowd_pct == 0` is a real value inside a restriction window**, not a missing one. An empty
   stadium is the treatment. The documented windows are each league's restricted season
   (for MLB, `{python} TREATED["mlb"][0]` only: every club admitted fans in `{python} TREATED["mlb"][1]`), the 2020 bubbles, and Canadian home
   games under the winter 2021–22 Omicron caps. Outside them, ESPN still reports zero attendance for
   `{python} thou(data_zero_nulled_total)` games (`{python} data_zero_nulled["nfl"]` NFL, `{python} data_zero_nulled["mlb"]` MLB, `{python} data_zero_nulled["nba"]` NBA, `{python} data_zero_nulled["nhl"]` NHL; `{python} data_zero_mlb_dh` of
   the MLB games are doubleheaders, meaning a second game by the same home team within twelve hours).
   We treat these as reporting artifacts and set their dose to
   missing, so the dose-response models drop them. The rule was written before the corrected tables
   were regenerated; @sec-zero reports what it changes.

   Inside the same restriction windows, ESPN
   also reports zero for games played after a team had already readmitted the public. A treated-season
   zero on or after a team's first game with fans (the earlier of its own first non-zero ESPN
   reading and a sourced public date) is treated as missing too; a documented re-closure keeps a
   zero real and nulls nothing. "Fans" means spectators from the general public, ticketed or invited
   as guests, including invited healthcare workers or first responders; team family, staff and
   broadcast media do not count, and no crowd-size threshold was added, because size is already
   carried by the dose itself.

   Two NHL teams, Nashville and St. Louis, never recorded a non-zero ESPN
   attendance all season, so their sourced dates reclassify all `{python} data_reopen_nsh_stl_n["NSH"]` of each
   team's treated-season home games; those sources describe the crowd as staff, family
   members and a handful of invited honorees or frontline workers, not a confirmed public audience.
   Two NFL teams' `fans_from` dates rest on comparably limited evidence: Green Bay's (2020-12-19)
   names invited healthcare workers and first responders, the same invited-guest class as
   Nashville and St. Louis; Philadelphia's (2020-10-18) names season-ticket members admitted in
   limited capacity, a public reopening rather than an invited-guest one.

   In total this reclassifies `{python} thou(data_reopen_nulled_total)` games (`{python} data_reopen_nulled["nfl"]` NFL,
   `{python} data_reopen_nulled["mlb"]` MLB, `{python} data_reopen_nulled["nba"]` NBA, `{python} data_reopen_nulled["nhl"]` NHL).
   `{python} thou(data_reopen_sourced_null)` of them are dated from a sourced entry and `{python} thou(data_reopen_unsourced_null)` from the
   data alone, for a team with no sourced entry; every audited team reached a documented verdict, so
   none are left unverified on the earlier, empty-stadium coding for lack of one. **This correction is not
   outcome-blind**: it was found through the literature comparison of @sec-lit, not the audit, and
   the fan definition above was fixed only after an unamended, scratch version of the rule had
   already been run and seen. @sec-zero reports what it changed; both versions are in
   `reopen_zero_sensitivity.csv`.
2. **A "normal" season is not dose 1.0.** Untreated-season mean dose is `{python} num(data_dose_ctrl_nfl, 2)` (NFL), `{python} num(data_dose_ctrl_nba, 2)` (NBA),
   `{python} num(data_dose_ctrl_nhl, 2)` (NHL), and **`{python} num(data_dose_ctrl_mlb, 2)` (MLB)**. Under this definition, a typical MLB game runs at roughly
   two-thirds of that park's best night of the year. Section [-@sec-mlb] shows that this single
   fact reorganizes what the MLB estimate can mean.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-dose
#| tbl-cap: "Crowd dose, treated versus control seasons, on the exclusion-masked sample (before listwise deletion of missing controls). The final column is the share of *normal-season* games whose dose falls inside the treated seasons' 5th–95th percentile range — that is, the degree to which the natural experiment is *not* a clean empty-versus-full contrast."
#| output: asis
o = overlap[overlap["scope"] == "all_treated"].set_index("sport").loc[SPORTS].reset_index()
out = pd.DataFrame({
    "League": [UP[s] for s in o["sport"]],
    "Treated mean dose": o["treated_mean"].map("{:.3f}".format),
    "Share of treated games fully empty": o["treated_share_zero"].map("{:.1%}".format),
    "Control mean dose": o["control_mean"].map("{:.3f}".format),
    "Control games inside treated 5–95% band": o["control_overlap"].map("{:.2%}".format),
    "n treated": o["n_treated"], "n control": o["n_control"],
})
display(md(out))
```

@tbl-dose is, in retrospect, the most consequential descriptive table in the paper. For `{python} words(data_n_leagues_low_overlap)`
leagues the treatment is a near-disjoint contrast: under 0.6% of normal games look anything like a
restricted game. For MLB, **`{python} pct(data_mlb_overlap_pooled, 1)`** of normal games fall inside the treated dose range. The
contamination is entirely 2021 (MLB's 2020 overlaps `{python} pct(data_mlb_overlap_2020, 2)`, no more than the NFL's `{python} pct(data_nfl_overlap, 2)`; its 2021
overlaps `{python} pct(data_mlb_overlap_2021, 1)` at a mean dose of `{python} num(data_mlb_treated_mean_2021, 3)`). MLB is running a different experiment from the other three
leagues, and @sec-mlb treats it accordingly.

The root cause is a gap between specification and implementation. The *design*
defines the treatment as policy capacity caps, while the *code* measures realized attendance over
empirical capacity. The two coincide wherever the cap binds (the NFL, NBA and NHL restricted
seasons) and diverge wherever it does not, which is baseball.

## Features and controls

Three controls enter every dose-response model in the main specification (the comparative interrupted-time-series estimator
in @sec-strategy uses raw means, with no controls), and they are computed identically for all four
leagues:

- **`elo_diff`**, the pre-game Elo rating difference, is the team-quality control. The
  implementation is a deliberate middle ground: a margin-of-victory multiplier of
  `ln(|margin| + 1)` without the autocorrelation correction of the full FiveThirtyEight
  specification, with home advantage and season-to-season carryover taken verbatim from published
  parameters and K rescaled where the simpler multiplier required it. Only the NBA's K was rescaled; the NHL's
  parameters transfer unchanged. NHL
  parameters follow @paine_nhl_elo. Stored ratings are strictly pre-game: a game's own result never enters its own
  stored rating. Out-of-sample accuracy is NBA `{python} dot(data_elo_acc_nba)` > NFL `{python} dot(data_elo_acc_nfl)` > NHL `{python} dot(data_elo_acc_nhl)` > MLB `{python} dot(data_elo_acc_mlb)`, the
  expected ordering, and not implausibly high for pre-game ratings. Elo accuracy is
  treated here as a bug gate, not a tuning target, because Elo enters only as a control variable.
- **`rest_diff`** is days since each team's previous game, differenced.
- **`away_travel_km`** is the great-circle distance from the away team's home venue.

Elo's internal home-advantage constant is held fixed and is never fan-adjusted. FiveThirtyEight's
MLB implementation uses a smaller home advantage for empty games; adopting that here would bake
the answer into the control.

Rest and travel are deliberately *not* baked into Elo, as some published implementations do; they
enter as separate regressors so they are not double-counted.

```{python}

#| include: false
desc_nfl_margin_pooled = pick(desc, sport="nfl", season="pooled_fullcrowd")["mean_home_margin"]
desc_nfl_margin_treated = pick(desc, sport="nfl", season=str(TREATED["nfl"][0]))["mean_home_margin"]
desc_nba_margin_pooled = pick(desc, sport="nba", season="pooled_fullcrowd")["mean_home_margin"]
desc_nba_margin_treated = pick(desc, sport="nba", season=str(TREATED["nba"][0]))["mean_home_margin"]
desc_mlb_margin_treated0 = pick(desc, sport="mlb", season=str(TREATED["mlb"][0]))["mean_home_margin"]
desc_mlb_margin_treated1 = pick(desc, sport="mlb", season=str(TREATED["mlb"][1]))["mean_home_margin"]
desc_mlb_margin_pooled = pick(desc, sport="mlb", season="pooled_fullcrowd")["mean_home_margin"]
desc_mlb_margin_se_pooled = pick(desc, sport="mlb", season="pooled_fullcrowd")["home_margin_se"]
desc_mlb_short_season = TREATED["mlb"][0]
desc_mlb_margin_se_2020 = pick(desc, sport="mlb", season=str(desc_mlb_short_season))["home_margin_se"]
_mlb_seasons = desc[(desc["sport"] == "mlb") & desc["season"].astype(str).str.isdigit()]
desc_mlb_neg_seasons = sorted(_mlb_seasons.loc[_mlb_seasons["mean_home_margin"] < 0, "season"].astype(str))
assert len(desc_mlb_neg_seasons) >= 2, "fewer than two negative MLB seasons; reword the descriptive-SE sentence"
desc_mlb_neg_years = ", ".join(desc_mlb_neg_seasons[:-1]) + " and " + desc_mlb_neg_seasons[-1]
desc_nhl_margin_treated = pick(desc, sport="nhl", season=str(TREATED["nhl"][0]))["mean_home_margin"]
desc_nhl_margin_pooled = pick(desc, sport="nhl", season="pooled_fullcrowd")["mean_home_margin"]

nhl_seasons = ["2018", "2019", "2020", "2021", "2022", "2023"]

desc_nhl_steps_total = len(_nhl_wp_diffs)
desc_nhl_steps_up = int((_nhl_wp_diffs > 0).sum())

_nhl_treated = str(TREATED["nhl"][0])
_nhl_untreated = [s for s in nhl_seasons if s != _nhl_treated]
desc_nhl_untreated_count = len(_nhl_untreated)
_nhl_coef = np.polyfit([int(s) for s in _nhl_untreated], [desc_nhl_wp[s] for s in _nhl_untreated], 1)
desc_nhl_trend_pred = np.polyval(_nhl_coef, int(_nhl_treated))
desc_nhl_trend_actual = desc_nhl_wp[_nhl_treated]
desc_nhl_trend_gap_se = (abs(desc_nhl_trend_actual - desc_nhl_trend_pred)
                          / pick(desc, sport="nhl", season=_nhl_treated)["home_win_se"])
```

Before any causal claim, we need the size of the thing being explained. @tbl-desc reports clean
regular-season home games only. Playoffs are excluded throughout the paper's main analysis
(@sec-playoffs revisits them descriptively), as are neutral-site games, relocated home venues and
the 2020 NBA and NHL bubbles.

![Home-field advantage by season, win percentage (top) and scoring margin (bottom). The shaded
band marks the 2020–21 restriction window; the exact treated season inside it differs by league.
Error bars are naive iid standard errors.](../results/figures/hfa_by_season.png){#fig-hfa}

Three things in @tbl-desc and @fig-hfa shape the rest of the paper.

**The NFL and NBA dip; MLB and the NHL do not.** NFL scoring margin falls from a pooled `{python} num(desc_nfl_margin_pooled, 2)` to
`{python} num(desc_nfl_margin_treated, 2)` in `{python} TREATED["nfl"][0]`; NBA margin falls from `{python} num(desc_nba_margin_pooled, 2)` to `{python} num(desc_nba_margin_treated, 2)` in `{python} TREATED["nba"][0]`. MLB's restricted seasons sit at `{python} num(desc_mlb_margin_treated0, 3)` and
`{python} num(desc_mlb_margin_treated1, 3)` against a pooled `{python} num(desc_mlb_margin_pooled, 3)`, *above* baseline, and the NHL's `{python} TREATED["nhl"][0]` margin of `{python} num(desc_nhl_margin_treated, 3)` is
indistinguishable from its `{python} num(desc_nhl_margin_pooled, 3)` baseline. As a check on the data, we expected home advantage to be
positive in full-crowd seasons and to dip in each league's restricted season. The NFL and NBA show
that pattern; MLB and the NHL do not dip, and on inspection neither exception points to a data
error. Both turned out to be informative, for different reasons in each league.

**MLB scoring margin is noise-dominated and cannot serve as MLB's primary descriptive signal.**
Pooled MLB home margin is `{python} sgn(desc_mlb_margin_pooled, 3)` runs with a standard error of `{python} num(desc_mlb_margin_se_pooled, 3)`; per-season standard errors
run around 0.09 in every season but the shortened `{python} desc_mlb_short_season` one (`{python} num(desc_mlb_margin_se_2020, 3)` there), and `{python} words(len(desc_mlb_neg_seasons))`
seasons' point estimates are negative (`{python} desc_mlb_neg_years`). The design's premise that margin buys
power over a binary outcome fails for baseball, where run differential is the noisiest
outcome in the study relative to its effect. For MLB, win percentage is the descriptive number to
read.

**Home advantage moves between seasons for reasons that have nothing to do with crowds.** The NHL
series drifts down across the whole window: `{python} dot(desc_nhl_wp["2018"])`, `{python} dot(desc_nhl_wp["2019"])`, `{python} dot(desc_nhl_wp["2020"])`, **`{python} dot(desc_nhl_wp["2021"])` (restricted)**, `{python} dot(desc_nhl_wp["2022"])`, `{python} dot(desc_nhl_wp["2023"])`.
This drift is *not* monotone: `{python} words(desc_nhl_steps_up)` of the `{python} words(desc_nhl_steps_total)` steps are increases, and the 2018→2019 step alone
is larger than the rest combined. The relevant fact is that a linear trend fitted through the `{python} words(desc_nhl_untreated_count)`
untreated seasons predicts a `{python} TREATED["nhl"][0]` win percentage of `{python} dot(desc_nhl_trend_pred, 4)` against an actual `{python} dot(desc_nhl_trend_actual, 4)`, a gap of
`{python} num(desc_nhl_trend_gap_se, 2)` standard errors. The restricted season sits *on* the trend through the NHL's untreated
seasons.
Section [-@sec-floor] shows that this between-season wobble is the binding constraint on the
whole design.

# Empirical strategy {#sec-strategy}

```{python}
#| label: strat-vars
#| include: false
from src.models.twfe import _prep

strat_nfl_coef_shipped = pick(sfe, sport="nfl", outcome="home_margin")["coef_shipped"]
strat_nfl_coef_seasonfe = pick(sfe, sport="nfl", outcome="home_margin")["coef_season_fe"]
strat_nba_coef_shipped = pick(sfe, sport="nba", outcome="home_margin")["coef_shipped"]
strat_nba_coef_seasonfe = pick(sfe, sport="nba", outcome="home_margin")["coef_season_fe"]
strat_nhl_win_shipped = pick(sfe, sport="nhl", outcome="home_win")["coef_shipped"]
strat_nhl_win_seasonfe = pick(sfe, sport="nhl", outcome="home_win")["coef_season_fe"]
strat_nhl_win_ratio = strat_nhl_win_seasonfe / strat_nhl_win_shipped
strat_mlb_coef_shipped = pick(sfe, sport="mlb", outcome="home_margin")["coef_shipped"]
strat_mlb_coef_seasonfe = pick(sfe, sport="mlb", outcome="home_margin")["coef_season_fe"]

strat_r2_nba = pick(sfe, sport="nba", outcome="home_margin")["collinearity_r2"]
strat_r2_nhl = pick(sfe, sport="nhl", outcome="home_margin")["collinearity_r2"]
strat_r2_mlb = pick(sfe, sport="mlb", outcome="home_margin")["collinearity_r2"]

# Per-season mean crowd_pct on the model (_prep) sample, split into each sport's normal
# and treated seasons from config — backs the "very nearly a season-level event" claim below.
_dose_cols = ["season", "crowd_pct", "neutral_site", "relocated_home", "is_bubble", "is_playoff",
              "home_elo", "away_elo", "home_rest_days", "away_rest_days"]
def _season_dose(sport):
    df = _prep(pd.read_parquet(ROOT / "data" / "processed" / f"{sport}.parquet", columns=_dose_cols))
    return df.groupby("season")["crowd_pct"].mean()

_strat_dose = {s: _season_dose(s) for s in SPORTS}

def _normal_range(sport):
    d = _strat_dose[sport]
    normal = d.drop(index=[y for y in TREATED[sport] if y in d.index])
    return normal.min(), normal.max()

strat_normal_lo_nfl, strat_normal_hi_nfl = _normal_range("nfl")
strat_normal_lo_nba, strat_normal_hi_nba = _normal_range("nba")
strat_normal_lo_nhl, strat_normal_hi_nhl = _normal_range("nhl")
strat_normal_lo_mlb, strat_normal_hi_mlb = _normal_range("mlb")

strat_treated_dose_nfl = _strat_dose["nfl"].loc[TREATED["nfl"][0]]
strat_treated_dose_nba = _strat_dose["nba"].loc[TREATED["nba"][0]]
strat_treated_dose_nhl = _strat_dose["nhl"].loc[TREATED["nhl"][0]]
strat_restricted_lo = min(strat_treated_dose_nfl, strat_treated_dose_nba, strat_treated_dose_nhl)
strat_restricted_hi = max(strat_treated_dose_nfl, strat_treated_dose_nba, strat_treated_dose_nhl)
strat_mlb_2021_dose = _strat_dose["mlb"].loc[TREATED["mlb"][1]]

_nhl_bubble = pd.read_parquet(ROOT / "data" / "processed" / "nhl.parquet",
                               columns=["is_bubble", "neutral_site", "is_playoff"])
_nhl_bubble = _nhl_bubble[_nhl_bubble["is_bubble"]]
assert _nhl_bubble["is_playoff"].all(), "some NHL bubble games are not playoff games; reword @sec-exclusions"

# MLB is the one league where a treated-season dummy is not near-collinear with dose; season FE
# nest that dummy, so the season-FE shift (in shipped SEs) is what adding it does to beta.
_sfe_mlb = sfe[sfe["sport"] == "mlb"]
strat_mlb_sfe_max_shift_se = ((_sfe_mlb["coef_season_fe"] - _sfe_mlb["coef_shipped"]).abs()
                              / _sfe_mlb["se_shipped"]).max()
assert strat_mlb_sfe_max_shift_se < 1, "MLB season-FE shift >= 1 SE; reword @sec-assumption"
assert (np.sign(_sfe_mlb["coef_season_fe"]) == np.sign(_sfe_mlb["coef_shipped"])).all(), \
    "MLB season-FE sign flipped; reword @sec-assumption"
strat_nhl_bubble_total = len(_nhl_bubble)
strat_nhl_bubble_neutral = int(_nhl_bubble["neutral_site"].sum())
strat_nhl_bubble_not_neutral = strat_nhl_bubble_total - strat_nhl_bubble_neutral
```

## The two estimators

We report two estimators side by side. Both were pre-specified; the second was originally
planned as a back-pocket robustness check. It was promoted to co-primary, before it was estimated,
once the treatment proved to be season-clustered.

**(a) Dose-response with team fixed effects.** For game $g$ played at home team $i$ in season $t$:

$$
y_{git} = \beta \cdot \text{crowd\_pct}_{g} + \gamma' X_{g} + \delta \cdot \text{trend}_{t} + \alpha_i + \varepsilon_{git}
$$

where $y$ is either home scoring margin or home win (as a linear probability model), $X$ is
`elo_diff`, `rest_diff`, `away_travel_km`, $\alpha_i$ are home-team fixed effects, and
$\text{trend}_t$ is a **linear** season index. Standard errors are clustered by home team.
$\beta$ is the object of interest: the change in the outcome per unit of crowd dose. Because the
win outcome is a linear probability model, $\beta$ on that outcome *is* a change in win
probability, which makes it the one unit comparable across four leagues that score in points, runs
and goals.

**(b) Comparative interrupted time series, away-team-as-control.** The raw, unadjusted version of
the same comparison: mean home advantage in full-crowd seasons minus mean home advantage in the
restricted season(s), with the treatment defined at *season* level from the configured labels.
Its crowd effect is signed so that positive means the crowd helps the home team, matching (a).
@fig-did shows the comparison it makes: each league's home advantage in full-crowd seasons against
its restricted season or seasons.

This estimator is often labeled a difference-in-differences, and we use that label only as
intuition. It is not a 2×2 DiD, because **no untreated group exists**: the pandemic reached every
team in every league simultaneously. What makes it a comparison at all is that the outcome is
already a difference: `home − away`. The **away team is the implicit control group**, and other
seasons are the control period. This nets out symmetric league-wide shifts (a scoring-environment
change that helps both sides equally leaves the margin untouched), but it does *not* net out a
home-specific 2020–21 shift. This is the same confound estimator (a) carries. **(b) is the
intuitive number, not the cleaner identification.**

## Why season fixed effects are left out {#sec-notwfe}

The natural instinct is to put full season dummies in the model alongside team fixed effects. It
is wrong here because of a structural property of this treatment. Leaving them out was not the original plan: the specification was first written with season
dummies, and the change described here was made after its first real-data run (@sec-intro).

Outside MLB, the crowd shock is very nearly a pure season-level event: normal-season mean dose
runs `{python} num(strat_normal_lo_nfl, 3)`–`{python} num(strat_normal_hi_nfl, 3)` in the NFL, `{python} num(strat_normal_lo_nba, 3)`–`{python} num(strat_normal_hi_nba, 3)` in the NBA and `{python} num(strat_normal_lo_nhl, 3)`–`{python} num(strat_normal_hi_nhl, 3)` in the NHL,
against `{python} num(strat_restricted_lo, 3)`–`{python} num(strat_restricted_hi, 3)` in each league's restricted season. MLB's normal seasons run lower
(`{python} num(strat_normal_lo_mlb, 3)`–`{python} num(strat_normal_hi_mlb, 3)`), and its 2021 season is only partially restricted (mean dose `{python} num(strat_mlb_2021_dose, 3)`).
Outside MLB, then, the per-unit coefficient is in practice an on/off contrast between restricted and
full-crowd seasons, scaled by the dose gap, rather than a dose-response curve; no league shows a
usable within-season dose curve (@tbl-within).

Full season dummies are therefore near-collinear with the treatment outside MLB: the R² of
`crowd_pct` on season and team fixed effects is `{python} dot(strat_r2_nfl)` (NFL), `{python} dot(strat_r2_nba)` (NBA) and `{python} dot(strat_r2_nhl)` (NHL), against `{python} dot(strat_r2_mlb)` (MLB),
and the season-FE coefficient is unstable. When we fit the two-way model anyway, the sign inverts in the
NFL (margin `{python} sgn(strat_nfl_coef_shipped, 2)` to `{python} sgn(strat_nfl_coef_seasonfe, 2)`) and the NBA (margin `{python} sgn(strat_nba_coef_shipped, 2)` to `{python} sgn(strat_nba_coef_seasonfe, 2)`); in the NHL it keeps its sign but grows to
`{python} times(strat_nhl_win_ratio, 1)` its shipped size (win probability, `{python} sgn(strat_nhl_win_shipped, 3)` to `{python} sgn(strat_nhl_win_seasonfe, 3)`); and in MLB, where the
collinearity is weakest, it also keeps its sign and moves toward zero (margin `{python} sgn(strat_mlb_coef_shipped, 2)` to `{python} sgn(strat_mlb_coef_seasonfe, 2)`).
@tbl-sfe in @sec-nhl reports the full season-FE sensitivity for every league and outcome.

The linear trend is the compromise: it nets out smooth drift in home advantage without erasing a
discrete one-season shock.

## Exclusions {#sec-exclusions}

Both estimators share one exclusion mask, applied identically in every league:

`neutral_site | relocated_home | is_bubble | is_playoff`

Neutral-site and relocated-home games are excluded because the "home" team is not at home: the
2020 Blue Jays in Buffalo, the 2021 Raptors in Tampa. Bubble games are excluded because the entire
regime differs (@sec-bubble). Playoff games are excluded because the higher seed hosts every NFL game before the neutral-site
Super Bowl and, in the NBA, NHL and MLB, the first game of every series and any deciding game
(and, in MLB's post-2022 Wild Card round, every game of it), so
playoff home advantage is contaminated by a quality asymmetry that regular-season home advantage is not.

The NHL bubble is identified by a **date rule**
(season 2020, from 1 August 2020), not by the neutral-site flag, and that implementation choice is load-bearing. Only `{python} strat_nhl_bubble_neutral` of the `{python} strat_nhl_bubble_total` NHL bubble
games carry ESPN's neutral-site flag. Toronto and Edmonton hosted the bubble as hub cities
[@nhl2020hubratify], and the flag is applied inconsistently across their games. Filtering
the bubble on `neutral_site` alone would miss `{python} strat_nhl_bubble_not_neutral` bubble games; they are
excluded from the main models regardless, since all `{python} strat_nhl_bubble_total` are also playoff games. The distinction matters only for
analyses that keep playoff games, such as the descriptive playoff table in @sec-playoffs.

## The identifying assumption {#sec-assumption}

Everything this paper estimates is:

$$
\hat\beta = \underbrace{\text{crowd effect}}_{\text{what we want}} \;+\; \underbrace{\text{any other 2020–21 league-wide, home-specific shift}}_{\text{what we cannot separate}}
$$

The linear trend removes *smooth* drift; it does not remove a *discrete* pandemic shock. A
treated-season dummy cannot usefully be added to separate the two: outside MLB it is
near-collinear with `crowd_pct`, and in MLB, where it is not, full season fixed effects (which
absorb it) keep both coefficients' signs and move them less than one standard error (@tbl-sfe). **There is no in-model separation, and nothing in this project
resolves it.** The 2020–21 seasons brought compressed schedules (outside the NFL), expanded rosters, altered
travel and testing protocols and, in baseball, outright rule changes. Any of these that moved
home advantage specifically, rather than scoring symmetrically, is inside our coefficient.

We investigated whether the NBA and NHL bubbles could break this identification apart and they
cannot; @sec-bubble reports that attempt and its failure.

# Results {#sec-results}

We report the two estimators together, then spend the rest of the section on what they can and
cannot resolve.

```{python}
# G3-18 fix: two-way (team x season) clustering of the frozen spec, refit live. The two-way
# SEs come back SMALLER than the shipped ones -- the estimator failing at six seasons, not a
# correction. "0.14-0.76x" in the old prose imported a different sensitivity (season FE) and
# does not reproduce here.
from linearmodels import PanelOLS
from src.models.twfe import _prep, CONTROLS
def _twoway_se(sport, outcome):
    d = _prep(pd.read_parquet(ROOT / "data" / "processed" / f"{sport}.parquet"))
    d = d[[outcome, "home_team", "season"] + CONTROLS].copy()
    d[outcome] = d[outcome].astype(float)
    d[CONTROLS] = d[CONTROLS].astype(float)
    d = d.dropna()
    d["season_trend"] = (d["season"] - d["season"].min()).astype(float)
    d = d.set_index(["home_team", "season"])
    r = PanelOLS(d[outcome], d[CONTROLS + ["season_trend"]], entity_effects=True).fit(
        cov_type="clustered", cluster_entity=True, cluster_time=True)
    return float(r.std_errors["crowd_pct"])
_tw = {(s, oc): _twoway_se(s, oc) / pick(twfe_all, sport=s, outcome=oc, sample="pooled")["se"]
       for s in SPORTS for oc in ("home_margin", "home_win")}
res_twoway_ratio_min, res_twoway_ratio_max = min(_tw.values()), max(_tw.values())
assert res_twoway_ratio_max < 1, "two-way SEs no longer smaller -- reword @sec-ri"

# G3-32 fix: calendar span of the treated seasons on the model (_prep) sample -- backs

_tw_dates = pd.concat([_prep(pd.read_parquet(ROOT / "data" / "processed" / f"{s}.parquet"))
                       .query("season in @TREATED[@s]")[["date"]] for s in SPORTS])
res_treated_span_months = (_tw_dates["date"].max() - _tw_dates["date"].min()).days / 30.44
```

## The two estimators, side by side

```{python}
#| label: tbl-main
#| tbl-cap: "Crowd effect on home advantage. (a) is the team-FE dose-response estimator, (b) the raw comparative interrupted time series. (a) is per unit of `crowd_pct`; (b) is the full-crowd minus restricted-season difference in home advantage, a level rather than a per-unit quantity. A positive value means the crowd advantages the home team. Standard errors clustered by home team (30–33 clusters). `n` is estimator (a)'s estimation sample; (b)'s is slightly larger, because (a) drops rows with a missing rest-day difference (a team's first game of a season) or a missing crowd reading."
#| output: asis
rows = []
for s in SPORTS:
    for oc, lab in [("home_margin", "Margin"), ("home_win", "Win prob.")]:
        a = pick(twfe_all, sport=s, outcome=oc, sample="pooled")
        b = pick(did_all, sport=s, outcome=oc, sample="pooled")
        d = 3 if oc == "home_margin" else 4
        rows.append({
            "League": UP[s], "Outcome": lab,
            "(a) coef (SE)": f"{a['coef']:+.{d}f} ({a['se']:.{d}f})",
            "(a) 95% CI": ci(a["ci_low"], a["ci_high"], d),
            "(b) coef (SE)": f"{b['crowd_effect']:+.{d}f} ({b['se']:.{d}f})",
            "(b) 95% CI": ci(b["ci_low"], b["ci_high"], d),
            "n": int(a["n_obs"]),
        })
display(md(pd.DataFrame(rows)))
```

![The intuitive picture: home advantage in full-crowd seasons versus the restricted season or
seasons (MLB has two), by league and outcome.](../results/figures/did_hfa_shrink.png){#fig-did}

![Dose-response crowd effect with 95% confidence intervals, both
outcomes.](../results/figures/twfe_crowd_effect.png){#fig-twfe}

Estimator (a) is per unit of dose and (b) is a level, so the like-for-like comparison is (b)
against (a) scaled by each league's dose gap, which is control-season minus restricted-season mean dose:
`{python} num(res_dose_gap["nfl"], 2)` (NFL), `{python} num(res_dose_gap["mlb"], 2)` (MLB), `{python} num(res_dose_gap["nba"], 2)` (NBA) and `{python} num(res_dose_gap["nhl"], 2)` (NHL).
The two agree in sign in `{python} words(res_coh_sign_agree)` of the eight cells. NHL margin disagrees
in sign, with (a) at `{python} sgn(res_nhl_margin_a, 3)` per unit against (b) at `{python} sgn(res_nhl_margin_b, 3)`, on a coefficient
indistinguishable from zero under either estimator (@sec-nhl). Where the sign agrees, the two are
close only in the NFL, where (b) is `{python} pct(abs(res_coh_rel[("nfl", "home_margin")]), 1)` smaller than scaled (a) on margin and
`{python} pct(res_coh_rel[("nfl", "home_win")], 1)` larger on win probability. Elsewhere they are far apart: (b) is
`{python} pct(abs(res_coh_rel[("nhl", "home_win")]), 0)` smaller in magnitude on NHL win probability, and larger in the NBA (by
`{python} pct(res_coh_rel[("nba", "home_margin")], 0)` on margin and `{python} pct(res_coh_rel[("nba", "home_win")], 0)` on win probability) and in MLB (by
`{python} pct(res_coh_rel[("mlb", "home_margin")], 0)` and `{python} pct(res_coh_rel[("mlb", "home_win")], 0)`). **Where they agree, the agreement is not
corroboration of identification.** Both estimators read the same between-season contrast and
both carry the confound of @sec-assumption. In the NFL, (b) matching scaled (a) is consistent with
the adjustments (controls, team fixed effects, trend) doing little net work there, a different and much smaller claim. In the NBA
and MLB the two are not interchangeable.

On the cross-league unit, win probability, the four point estimates are:

```{python}
c = csv("twfe_cross_sport")
c = c[c["sample"] == "pooled"].set_index("sport").loc[SPORTS].reset_index()
out = pd.DataFrame({
    "League": [UP[s] for s in c["sport"]],
    "Δ win prob. per unit dose": c["coef"].map("{:+.4f}".format),
```

Every interval crosses zero. The NFL has the only appreciable point estimate, `{python} sgn(res_nfl_winprob_pp, 1)`
