We therefore do not present it as suggestive evidence standing alone.

We do not rely on these p-values, because Section [-@sec-ri] shows that the design's
p-value floor under randomization inference is `{python} num(res_ri_floor_min, 3)`.

## What this design can detect {#sec-power}

The minimum detectable effect at 80% power and two-sided $\alpha = .05$ is approximately
$2.8 \times \text{SE}$. Setting that against each league's *entire* measured home advantage gives
the central table of this paper.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-mde
#| tbl-cap: "Minimum detectable effect against total home-field advantage. Total HFA is the pooled full-crowd descriptive value: mean home margin, or home win percentage minus .500. The two right-hand columns differ only in scaling and are explained below."
#| output: asis
inp = meta[meta["scope"] == "input"].set_index("sport")
rows = []
# control-season mean dose, for the rescaled column
dose = overlap[overlap["scope"] == "all_treated"].set_index("sport")["control_mean"]
for s in SPORTS:
    p = pick(desc, sport=s, season="pooled_fullcrowd")
    hfa = {"home_margin": p["mean_home_margin"], "home_win": p["home_win_pct"] - 0.5}
    for oc, lab in [("home_margin", "Margin"), ("home_win", "Win prob.")]:
        se = pick(twfe_all, sport=s, outcome=oc, sample="pooled")["se"]
        mde = 2.8 * se
        rows.append({
            "League": UP[s], "Outcome": lab,
            "MDE (80% power)": f"{mde:.3f}",
            "Total HFA": f"{hfa[oc]:.3f}",
            "MDE ÷ HFA (per unit dose)": f"{mde / hfa[oc]:.2f}×",
            "MDE ÷ HFA (rescaled)": f"{mde * dose[s] / hfa[oc]:.2f}×",
        })
display(md(pd.DataFrame(rows)))
```

Read the "MDE ÷ HFA (per unit dose)" column first. **In all eight cells, the smallest crowd effect this study could
reliably detect exceeds the whole of that league's home-field advantage, the smallest margin of
exceedance (`{python} intro_min_ratio_label`) by `{python} pct(intro_mde_min_ratio - 1, 0)`.** A
crowd effect that explained *all* of home advantage would, at this per-unit scaling, more likely
than not go undetected in `{python} words(intro_power_lt_half_count)` of the eight cells, and in
`{python} words(intro_power_lt_half_rescaled_count)` once rescaled to each league's normal-season dose.

The caveat weighs as much as the finding, so we state it at equal volume. **The coefficient is scaled
per unit of `crowd_pct`, and no league's data spans a full unit.** Control-season mean dose is `{python} num(data_dose_ctrl_nfl, 2)`
(NFL), `{python} num(data_dose_ctrl_mlb, 2)` (MLB), `{python} num(data_dose_ctrl_nba, 2)` (NBA), `{python} num(data_dose_ctrl_nhl, 2)` (NHL), against treated means of `{python} num(res_dose_treated_nfl, 3)`, `{python} num(res_dose_treated_mlb, 3)`, `{python} num(res_dose_treated_nba, 3)` and `{python} num(res_dose_treated_nhl, 3)`.
A crowd effect explaining 100% of home advantage therefore implies a per-unit coefficient of
HFA ÷ control dose, not HFA itself. Rescaling to each league's normal-season dose (the sixth
column) brings three cells close to one: NBA win probability to `{python} num(res_mde_rescaled_nba_win, 2)`,
MLB win probability to `{python} num(res_mde_rescaled_mlb_win, 2)` and NBA margin to `{python} num(res_mde_rescaled_nba_margin, 2)`. The
remaining five run from `{python} num(res_mde_rescaled_nhl_margin, 2)` (NHL margin, down from `{python} num(res_mde_unscaled_nhl_margin, 2)`) to `{python} num(res_mde_rescaled_mlb_margin, 2)` (MLB margin).

So the `{python} words(intro_mde_gt1_count)`-of-eight statement is correct **at per-unit scaling** and is **not robust to
rescaling**: the three smallest rescaled ratios sit at `{python} num(res_mde_rescaled_nba_margin, 2)` or below, and the other five exceed one by `{python} pct(res_mde_rescaled_nhl_margin - 1, 0)` or
more. Any use of this ratio must name which scaling it is quoting. The qualitative claim survives
either scaling, and it is all we actually need: this design's resolution is on the same order
as the entire quantity it is trying to decompose.

The same arithmetic has a third consequence, for a headline number this time: **MLB's coefficient extrapolates roughly `{python} times(res_mlb_extrapolation, 1)` beyond the dose baseball typically
attains.** It reads a 0→1 contrast off an empty-to-typical-full contrast of 0→`{python} num(data_dose_ctrl_mlb, 2)`.

## Randomization inference over `{python} words(intro_n_seasons)` seasons {#sec-ri}

The clustered standard errors in @tbl-main are computed over `{python} thou(res_n_obs_min)` to `{python} thou(res_n_obs_max)` game-level
observations. This is the wrong denominator, and it is wrong in a way that flatters us.

The treatment was not assigned to games. It was assigned to *seasons*: one shock, delivered
league-wide, once. The design has **`{python} words(intro_n_seasons)`** season-level assignments to
compare: the `{python} words(intro_n_seasons)` seasons in the panel (for MLB, `{python} words(intro_n_seasons - len(TREATED["mlb"]) + 1)`: each treated season is ranked against the `{python} words(intro_n_seasons - len(TREATED["mlb"]))` untreated ones). Clustering by season is not the fix (`{python} words(intro_n_seasons)` clusters is far
below the ~40 that cluster-robust variance estimation needs; the two-way (team × season) clustered attempt
returns standard errors `{python} times(res_twoway_ratio_min, 2)` to `{python} times(res_twoway_ratio_max, 2)` the size of the shipped ones, which is the
estimator breaking rather than a correction).

The appropriate inference is randomization-based. We re-estimate the model with each season in
turn wearing the treatment label, and ask where the actual treated season falls in that reference
distribution.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ri
#| tbl-cap: "Randomization inference over season-level treatment assignment. Deviations are season indicator coefficients from a model with team fixed effects and a linear season trend. The floor is 1/(1 + number of placebo assignments). Treated deviations are signed (negative = lower home advantage in the treated season, i.e. a positive crowd effect); the untreated column is the largest absolute deviation; the test is two-sided on |deviation|. For MLB the more extreme treated year is ranked against single-season placebos."
#| output: asis
rows = []
for s in SPORTS:
    for oc, lab in [("home_margin", "Margin"), ("home_win", "Win prob.")]:
        g = seasonfx[(seasonfx["sport"] == s) & (seasonfx["outcome"] == oc)]
        tr = g[g["is_treated"]]
        d = 3 if oc == "home_margin" else 4
        rows.append({
            "League": UP[s], "Outcome": lab,
            "Treated-season deviation": " / ".join(f"{v:+.{d}f}" for v in tr["coef"]),
            "Largest untreated deviation": f"{g[~g['is_treated']]['coef'].abs().max():.{d}f}",
            "RI p": f"{g['ri_pvalue'].iloc[0]:.3f}",
            "RI p floor": f"{g['ri_pvalue_floor'].iloc[0]:.3f}",
        })
display(md(pd.DataFrame(rows)))
```

Two readings follow.

**No randomization-inference p-value in this study falls below `{python} num(res_ri_pvalue_min, 3)`, and the floor of the
procedure is `{python} num(res_ri_floor_min, 3)`** (`{python} num(res_ri_floor_mlb, 3)` for MLB, which has `{python} words(len(TREATED["mlb"]))` treated seasons). *No result this design is
capable of producing could reach conventional significance under randomization inference.* This is
a property of a design with only `{python} words(intro_n_seasons)` season-level assignments.

**Ordinary season-to-season variation in home advantage exceeds the COVID signal.** The NFL's 2018
season deviates `{python} sgn(res_nfl_season2018_dev, 3)` points of home margin from trend; its treated `{python} TREATED["nfl"][0]` season deviates
`{python} sgn(res_nfl_season_treated_dev, 3)`. An untreated season moved home advantage twice as far as the pandemic did, in the opposite
direction, for reasons this study cannot identify.

## Why more seasons would not help {#sec-floor}

The obvious response is to extend the panel. It would not work, for a structural reason.

Decompose the observed between-season spread in home advantage into sampling noise and genuine
between-season variation, and construct a noise floor from the two components that do *not* shrink
as control seasons are added: the treated season's own sampling error (2020 happened once, and no
number of control seasons makes it happen twice) and $\text{sd}_{\text{true}}$, real
season-to-season variation in home advantage.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-floor
#| tbl-cap: "The noise floor. All quantities are on the season-dummy / outcome-level basis — margin points and win-probability points, the same units as home advantage. **This is a different basis from @tbl-mde**, whose ratios are per unit of `crowd_pct`. † marks cells where observed between-season spread fell below average sampling noise and the decomposition clamped at zero; read those as *undetectably small*, not *zero*."
#| output: asis
rows = []
for s in SPORTS:
    for oc, lab in [("home_margin", "Margin"), ("home_win", "Win prob.")]:
        r = pick(noise, sport=s, outcome=oc)
        rows.append({
            "League": UP[s], "Outcome": lab,
            "sd(true between-season)": f"{r['sd_true']:.4f}" + (" †" if r["sd_true_censored"] else ""),
            "Treated-season SE": f"{r['treated_se']:.4f}",
            "Total HFA": f"{r['hfa']:.4f}",
            "MDE ÷ HFA (naive)": f"{r['ratio_naive']:.2f}×",
            "MDE ÷ HFA (floor)": f"{r['ratio_floor']:.2f}×",
        })
display(md(pd.DataFrame(rows)))
```

The floor ratio is at or above 1.0 in `{python} words(res_floor_ge1_count)` of eight cells, a
different count from @tbl-mde's `{python} words(intro_mde_gt1_count)`, on a **different basis**. The
two tables must never be quoted side by side without naming their scaling.
The one cell below 1.0 is MLB win probability (`{python} times(pick(noise, sport="mlb", outcome="home_win")["ratio_floor"], 2)`), where the decomposition clamped at
zero (†), so its floor is a lower bound. NBA win probability, whose team-clustered interval excludes a
full-advantage effect, rises from `{python} times(pick(noise, sport="nba", outcome="home_win")["ratio_naive"], 2)` to `{python} times(pick(noise, sport="nba", outcome="home_win")["ratio_floor"], 2)` once season-level variation is admitted.

The decisive number in @tbl-floor is the NFL's: genuine between-season variation in NFL home
margin is **`{python} num(res_noise_nfl_sd_true, 2)` points, essentially the whole of the NFL's `{python} num(res_noise_nfl_hfa, 2)`-point home advantage.** Home advantage
in football wobbles by about its own size, season to season, for non-crowd reasons. Against
that backdrop, one treated season cannot identify a crowd effect of plausible magnitude no matter
how many control seasons flank it.

Two further consequences follow, and both cut against us:

- The ratio of the honest floor to the naive clustered MDE runs from `{python} num(res_floor_over_naive_min, 2)` to `{python} num(res_floor_over_naive_max, 2)`, never below
  1.00, which holds **by construction**. In the `{python} words(res_floor_measured_count)` cells
  where genuine between-season variation is measurably non-zero it rises to `{python} num(res_floor_over_naive_measured_min, 2)`–`{python} num(res_floor_over_naive_measured_max, 2)`; in the
  `{python} words(res_floor_censored_count)` cells where the decomposition clamped at zero (†) it is
  exactly 1.00. **Admitting season-level shocks therefore never improves inference, and materially
  worsens it in half the cells: the team-clustered season-level standard errors are, if anything,
  optimistic.**
- Extending the panel would not make randomization inference decisive. More seasons lower the
  $1/k$ p-value floor, but @tbl-ri shows an untreated season already deviating further than the
  treated one in every cell, so added seasons would move the p-value toward the treated season's current middling rank,
  not toward zero.

**Recommendation on record: extending the panel is not worth its cost for this question.**

## Pooling does not tighten the answer {#sec-pool}

With four leagues and four estimates, the obvious temptation is to pool them and read a tighter
interval.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-meta
#| tbl-cap: "Cross-league pooling of the win-probability estimates."
#| output: asis
m = meta[meta["scope"] != "input"].copy()
out = pd.DataFrame({
    "Set": ["4 leagues" if r == "4sport" else "3 leagues (ex-NHL)" for r in m["scope"]],
    "Method": ["Fixed-effect (inverse-variance)" if x == "fe" else "Random-effects (DerSimonian–Laird)" for x in m["method"]],
    "Pooled Δ win prob.": m["coef"].map("{:+.5f}".format),
    "SE": m["se"].map("{:.5f}".format),
    "95% CI": [ci(a, b, 4) for a, b in zip(m["ci_low"], m["ci_high"])],
    "Q (p)": [f"{q:.2f} ({p:.3f})" for q, p in zip(m["q"], m["q_pvalue"])],
    "I²": m["i2"].map("{:.1%}".format),
})
display(md(out))
```

The pooled estimates are essentially zero. The four-league fixed-effect estimate is about `{python} num(res_meta_se_over_coef_4fe, 1)` times
smaller than its own standard error, and the random-effects one about `{python} num(res_meta_se_over_coef_4re, 0)` times smaller. The
four-league confidence interval is `{python} pct(res_meta_narrower_fe, 1)` narrower than the three-league one on a
fixed-effect basis, `{python} pct(res_meta_narrower_re, 1)` narrower on a random-effects basis. We report all of this and then
decline to lean on any of it, for three reasons.

**First, the four estimates share a bias, not merely independent noise.** Each one is
*crowd effect + that league's own 2020–21 non-crowd home-specific shift*. Inverse-variance pooling
shrinks *sampling* error at rate $1/\sqrt{k}$ and does exactly nothing to a bias common across all
four leagues: the same pandemic, the same empty buildings, the same travel and testing protocols,
in the same `{python} words(round(res_treated_span_months))` months. **Any pooled standard error here is a lower bound on the real uncertainty**,
and no statement of the form "the pooled interval rules out effects larger than X" is licensed by
this table.

**Second, the heterogeneity statistics carry no information at $k = `{python} len(SPORTS)`$.** The Q test would need
to exceed `{python} num(res_meta_q_crit, 2)` to reject; it observed `{python} num(res_meta_q_4sport, 2)`. A test with no power cannot show that the
effects are homogeneous. $I^2$ fell from `{python} pct(res_meta_i2_3sport, 1)` to `{python} pct(res_meta_i2_4sport, 1)` when the NHL was added, mechanically, because
the NHL estimate landed near the pooled mean. Section [-@sec-mlb] argues on substantive grounds
that the true per-league effects are *not* common, which is the opposite of what a naive reading
of $I^2$ would suggest.

**Third, the gain is specification-dependent.** It is `{python} pct(res_meta_narrower_fe, 1)` or `{python} pct(res_meta_narrower_re, 1)` depending on which pooling model
one prefers, with the fixed-effect point estimate "moving" from `{python} sgn(res_meta_coef_3sport_fe, 4)` to `{python} sgn(res_meta_coef_4sport_fe, 4)`, a movement
entirely inside noise.

# League-by-league {#sec-leagues}

The design treats sport as a parameter, but the `{python} words(len(SPORTS))` leagues did not receive the same experiment,
and each needs its own discussion.

## NFL: the largest estimate, resting on one control season {#sec-loso}

```{python}
#| label: leagues-loso-vars
#| include: false
lg_nfl_margin = pick(twfe_all, sport="nfl", outcome="home_margin", sample="pooled")["coef"]
_loso_nfl = loso[loso["sport"] == "nfl"]
lg_loso_nfl_2018_win_delta_se = pick(_loso_nfl, outcome="home_win", dropped_season=2018)["delta_over_se_base"]
lg_loso_nfl_2018_win_coef = pick(_loso_nfl, outcome="home_win", dropped_season=2018)["coef"]
lg_loso_nfl_max_other = _loso_nfl[_loso_nfl["dropped_season"] != 2018]["delta_over_se_base"].abs().max()
_loso_mlb = loso[loso["sport"] == "mlb"]
lg_loso_mlb_max = _loso_mlb.loc[_loso_mlb["delta_over_se_base"].abs().idxmax(), "delta_over_se_base"]
_loso_nba = loso[loso["sport"] == "nba"]
lg_loso_nba_max = _loso_nba.loc[_loso_nba["delta_over_se_base"].abs().idxmax(), "delta_over_se_base"]
_loso_nhl = loso[loso["sport"] == "nhl"]
lg_loso_nhl_max = _loso_nhl.loc[_loso_nhl["delta_over_se_base"].abs().idxmax(), "delta_over_se_base"]
```

The NFL produces the study's largest point estimate: `{python} sgn(lg_nfl_margin, 2)` points of margin, `{python} sgn(res_nfl_winprob_pp, 1)` percentage points
of win probability, an estimate @sec-power shows this design cannot resolve from zero. It is also
the estimate most sensitive to the composition of the control window.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-loso
#| tbl-cap: "NFL leave-one-season-out: each *untreated* season dropped in turn from the frozen specification."
#| output: asis
g = loso[loso["sport"] == "nfl"]
piv = g.pivot(index="outcome", columns="dropped_season", values="coef")
base = g.groupby("outcome")["coef_base"].first()
rows = []
for oc, lab, d in [("home_margin", "Margin", 3), ("home_win", "Win prob.", 4)]:
    r = {"Outcome": lab, "Base": f"{base[oc]:+.{d}f}"}
    for c in piv.columns:
        r[f"drop {c}"] = f"{piv.loc[oc, c]:+.{d}f}"
    rows.append(r)
display(md(pd.DataFrame(rows)))
```

Dropping 2018 moves the win-probability estimate by `{python} sgn(lg_loso_nfl_2018_win_delta_se, 2)` base standard errors, from `{python} sgn(res_nfl_winprob_pp / 100, 3)` to
`{python} sgn(lg_loso_nfl_2018_win_coef, 3)`. No other season moves either outcome by more than `{python} num(lg_loso_nfl_max_other, 1)` SE. The NHL alone is stable
under the same exercise (`{python} num(abs(lg_loso_nhl_max), 2)` SE); MLB and the NBA both move about two-thirds of a standard
error (`{python} num(abs(lg_loso_mlb_max), 2)` and `{python} num(abs(lg_loso_nba_max), 2)` SE respectively).

This has to be read with both halves. It is **partly genuine fragility**: the NFL result does
lean on one unusually home-friendly control season, the same 2018 that @tbl-ri flags as deviating
`{python} sgn(res_nfl_season2018_dev, 2)` points. It is also **partly mechanical**, because 2018 is an endpoint of a `{python} words(intro_n_seasons)`-season panel, and
dropping an endpoint tilts the linear trend that the specification fits. A quadratic trend moves the
estimate the same way, and @sec-trend shows it is this same fragility again. The
consequence is narrow and we hold to it: this removes the basis for describing the NFL point
estimate as suggestive evidence in its own right.

This analysis was added after the main results were known, so its legitimacy needs stating:
leave-one-season-out is **exhaustive and mechanical**. Every untreated season is dropped exactly
once and there is no researcher choice inside the procedure, so there is nothing to fit to a
desired answer.

## NBA: the bubble cannot disentangle the channels {#sec-bubble}

```{python}
#| label: leagues-bubble-vars
#| include: false
_nba_raw = pd.read_parquet(ROOT / "data" / "processed" / "nba.parquet")
_seed_preview = _nba_raw[_nba_raw["is_bubble"].fillna(False) & ~_nba_raw["is_playoff"].fillna(False)]
lg_bubble_teams = len(set(_seed_preview["home_team"]) | set(_seed_preview["away_team"]))
lg_bubble_seed_n = len(_seed_preview)
# The tbl-bubble caption below types this count rather than computing it: fail loudly if it moves.
assert lg_bubble_seed_n == 88, f"tbl-bubble caption says 88 restart games, data says {lg_bubble_seed_n}"
_nhl_raw = pd.read_parquet(ROOT / "data" / "processed" / "nhl.parquet")
lg_nhl_bubble_n = len(_nhl_raw[_nhl_raw["is_bubble"].fillna(False)])
```

The 2020 NBA restart at Walt Disney World is superficially the perfect complement to the empty-stadium
experiment. `{python} words(lg_bubble_teams).capitalize()` teams played `{python} thou(lg_bubble_seed_n)` seeding games and a full postseason at a single
neutral site, with a designated "home" team for each game. If "home" without a crowd *and* without
travel still shows an advantage, the residual is familiarity and convention; if it shows none, the
crowd looks larger.

We ran the decomposition and the placebo. Both are reported here, and neither supports an
inference.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bubble
#| tbl-cap: "NBA home advantage by regime, computed inline; regular-season games only. Bubble seeding games are the 88 restart games with `is_playoff == False`."
#| output: asis
nba = pd.read_parquet(ROOT / "data" / "processed" / "nba.parquet")
b = nba[nba["is_bubble"].fillna(False)]
seed = b[~b["is_playoff"].fillna(False)]
full = pick(desc, sport="nba", season="pooled_fullcrowd")
empty = pick(desc, sport="nba", season="2021")

def cell(n, m, se, w, wse):
    return dict(n=int(n), margin=f"{m:+.3f} ({se:.3f})", win=f"{w:.3f} ({wse:.3f})")

sm, sse = seed["home_margin"].mean(), seed["home_margin"].std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(seed))
sw = seed["home_win"].mean(); swse = np.sqrt(sw * (1 - sw) / len(seed))
lg_bubble_ci_lo = sm - 1.96 * sse
lg_bubble_ci_hi = sm + 1.96 * sse
lg_bubble_full_minus_seed = full["mean_home_margin"] - sm
lg_bubble_seed_minus_empty = sm - empty["mean_home_margin"]
rows = [
    {"Regime": "Full crowd, own arena (untreated seasons)",
     **cell(full["n_games"], full["mean_home_margin"], full["home_margin_se"],
            full["home_win_pct"], full["home_win_se"])},
    {"Regime": "Bubble seeding games (no crowd, no travel, neutral court)",
     **cell(len(seed), sm, sse, sw, swse)},
    {"Regime": "Empty / capped, own arena (2021)",
     **cell(empty["n_games"], empty["mean_home_margin"], empty["home_margin_se"],
            empty["home_win_pct"], empty["home_win_se"])},
]
out = pd.DataFrame(rows).rename(columns={"n": "n games", "margin": "Home margin (SE)",
                                         "win": "Home win % (SE)"})
display(md(out))
```

The **seeding placebo** asks whether a bubble game shows any home advantage at all. It returns
`{python} sgn(sm, 2)` points on `{python} thou(lg_bubble_seed_n)` games with a standard error of `{python} num(sse, 2)`, an interval of roughly `{python} civ(lg_bubble_ci_lo, lg_bubble_ci_hi, 1)`. That
interval contains zero *and* it contains the NBA's full normal home advantage of `{python} num(full["mean_home_margin"], 2)`. **It is a
test that cannot fail**, and reporting it as evidence in either direction would be an abuse of it.

The **decomposition** fares no better, because its bubble-to-empty ordering runs backwards. Full crowd minus bubble is `{python} sgn(lg_bubble_full_minus_seed, 2)` points, in the expected direction. But
bubble minus empty is `{python} sgn(lg_bubble_seed_minus_empty, 2)`, so the empty-arena regime shows *less* home advantage than the bubble
regime, when the bubble strips away travel and court familiarity on top of the crowd.

Three structural problems compound the arithmetic ones, and they are why we do not attempt to
rehabilitate this analysis:

1. **The bubble sits inside the pandemic window.** It swaps one bundled treatment for a different
   bundled treatment, which leaves no clean counterfactual.
2. **Bubble "home" was not nothing.** The designated home team got most of the virtual fans on
   the arena video boards, home-leaning in-venue announcing, and piped-in crowd noise adjusted at
   home teams' request [@nba2020virtualfans]. The bubble's null is not cleanly a zero.
3. **The NHL bubble cannot substitute.** All `{python} thou(lg_nhl_bubble_n)` NHL bubble games are playoff games, therefore
   quality-confounded, so they feed neither a placebo (which requires regular-season games) nor a
   regular-season decomposition.

We report the table, and we draw no inference from it. The identification problem in
@sec-assumption stands unresolved.

## NHL: strongest treatment, weakest specification defense {#sec-nhl}

```{python}
#| label: leagues-nhl-vars
#| include: false
from src.models.twfe import fit
lg_nhl_margin = pick(twfe_all, sport="nhl", outcome="home_margin", sample="pooled")
lg_nhl_win = pick(twfe_all, sport="nhl", outcome="home_win", sample="pooled")
lg_nhl_zero_share = pick(overlap, sport="nhl", scope="all_treated")["treated_share_zero"]
lg_nba_win_coef = pick(twfe_all, sport="nba", outcome="home_win", sample="pooled")["coef"]
_w22 = fit(_nhl_raw, "home_win", sample="treated", treated_seasons=[2022], trend="none")
lg_nhl_within2022_win = _w22["coef"]
# prose says "Neither fit is distinguishable from zero" (within-2022 and within-2021, win prob.).
assert _w22["pvalue"] > 0.05 and pick(within, sport="nhl", outcome="home_win")["pvalue"] > 0.05, \
    "reword 'Neither fit is distinguishable from zero' in @sec-nhl"

# "smallest estimate" held for both outcomes at the frozen
# numbers but no longer does for win probability (NBA is now smaller). Check both live.
_pooled_by_sport = {s: pick(twfe_all, sport=s, outcome="home_margin", sample="pooled")["coef"] for s in SPORTS}
assert min(_pooled_by_sport, key=lambda s: abs(_pooled_by_sport[s])) == "nhl", \
    "NHL margin is no longer the study's smallest-magnitude margin estimate; reword @sec-nhl"
_pooled_win_by_sport = {s: pick(twfe_all, sport=s, outcome="home_win", sample="pooled")["coef"] for s in SPORTS}
assert min(_pooled_win_by_sport, key=lambda s: abs(_pooled_win_by_sport[s])) == "nba", \
    "NBA win probability is no longer the study's smallest-magnitude win estimate; reword @sec-nhl"
# "smallest margin estimate relative to its own home advantage" -- |coef| / pooled full-crowd HFA margin.
_rel_margin = {s: abs(_pooled_by_sport[s]) / pick(desc, sport=s, season="pooled_fullcrowd")["mean_home_margin"] for s in SPORTS}
assert min(_rel_margin, key=_rel_margin.get) == "nhl", \
    "NHL margin is no longer the smallest margin estimate relative to its own HFA; reword @sec-nhl"
# the prose says the NFL two-way (season FE) win-probability CI excludes zero on the wrong side.
lg_nfl_sfe_win = pick(sfe, sport="nfl", outcome="home_win")
assert lg_nfl_sfe_win["ci_high_season_fe"] < 0, "NFL season-FE win CI no longer below zero; reword @sec-nhl"
```

The NHL has the study's most complete empty-arena treatment (`{python} pct(lg_nhl_zero_share, 0)` of treated games at zero
attendance, mean dose `{python} num(res_dose_treated_nhl, 3)`) and returns the study's smallest margin estimate in magnitude relative to its own home advantage,
`{python} sgn(lg_nhl_margin["coef"], 3)` goals; on win probability it is `{python} sgn(lg_nhl_win["coef"], 3)`, edged
below by the NBA's `{python} sgn(lg_nba_win_coef, 3)`. Its win-probability interval, `{python} civ(lg_nhl_win["ci_low"], lg_nhl_win["ci_high"], 3)`, **contains both the NFL's
`{python} sgn(res_nfl_winprob_pp / 100, 3)` and the NBA's `{python} sgn(lg_nba_win_coef, 3)`**. It cannot distinguish zero from an NFL-sized effect, so it is
consistent with the other leagues' estimates rather than an independent confirmation of them.
Estimator (b) returns `{python} sgn(res_nhl_margin_b, 3)` on margin against (a)'s `{python} sgn(res_nhl_margin_a, 3)`,
opposite signs on a coefficient neither estimator can distinguish from zero.

Four diagnostics are reported here whichever way they came out. Only the travel test was
pre-committed when the NHL was added; the trend, season-fixed-effects and within-season analyses
were added during review.

**Trend sensitivity.** The linear season trend is not absorbing the treatment:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-trend
#| tbl-cap: "NHL trend sensitivity."
#| output: asis
g = trend[trend["sport"] == "nhl"]
rows = []
for oc, lab, d in [("home_margin", "Margin", 4), ("home_win", "Win prob.", 4)]:
    r = {"Outcome": lab}
    for t in ["none", "linear", "quadratic"]:
        x = pick(g, outcome=oc, trend=t)
        r[t] = f"{x['coef']:+.{d}f} ({x['se']:.{d}f})"
    rows.append(r)
display(md(pd.DataFrame(rows).rename(columns={"none": "No trend", "linear": "Linear (shipped)",
                                              "quadratic": "Quadratic"})))
```

Removing the trend entirely moves the win-probability estimate by roughly a fifth of a standard
error.

**Travel.** The 2020–21 NHL season was played in four realigned divisions, including an
all-Canadian North Division [@nhl2020realignment], which mechanically changed the travel
distribution in exactly the treated season. The league and players' union state that the closure
of the U.S.–Canada border required the realignment and that they sought to minimize travel
[@nhl2020seasonplan]. If crowd
and travel fell together, `away_travel_km` could be absorbing the crowd effect. It is not. The
correlation between dose and away travel within the treated season is `{python} num(pick(travel, outcome="home_margin")["corr_crowd_travel_treated"], 3)`, and dropping the
control moves the coefficient by `{python} sgn(pick(travel, outcome="home_margin")["delta"], 4)` (margin, from `{python} sgn(pick(travel, outcome="home_margin")["coef_with_travel"], 4)` to `{python} sgn(pick(travel, outcome="home_margin")["coef_without_travel"], 4)`) and `{python} sgn(pick(travel, outcome="home_win")["delta"], 4)` (win probability). Those shifts are `{python} num(pick(travel, outcome="home_margin")["delta"] / lg_nhl_margin["se"], 2)` and `{python} num(pick(travel, outcome="home_win")["delta"] / lg_nhl_win["se"], 2)` of the respective shipped standard errors, with the
estimation sample identical at `{python} thou(pick(travel, outcome="home_margin")["n_obs_with_travel"])` games in both fits, though on margin the shift is also about `{python} pct(pick(travel, outcome="home_margin")["delta"] / lg_nhl_margin["coef"], 0)` of the coefficient itself.

**The 2022 control season is imperfect, and in a direction that is conservative.** Omicron reduced
attendance sharply for Canadian teams from December 2021 through February 2022: mean dose 0.519,
with 26 near-empty games. The configuration deliberately leaves 2022 untreated. The continuous
dose variable is *correct* for those games (it records what it should), and only the season-level
labeling used by estimator (b) is imprecise. This affects roughly 1–2% of the control mass and
biases toward zero. Marking all of 2022 as treated would be worse: it would break the
self-anchoring capacity definition of @sec-dose.

**Season fixed effects, and the rebuttal.** The NHL is where the argument of @sec-notwfe is at its
weakest.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-sfe
#| tbl-cap: "Season-fixed-effects sensitivity. Collinearity R² is from regressing `crowd_pct` on season and home-team dummies; it is approximate by construction, computed on 1–6% more rows than the fit, which moves it by at most 0.0023."
#| output: asis
rows = []
for s in SPORTS:
    for oc, lab, d in [("home_margin", "Margin", 3), ("home_win", "Win prob.", 4)]:
        r = pick(sfe, sport=s, outcome=oc)
        rows.append({
            "League": UP[s], "Outcome": lab,
            "Shipped (team FE + trend)": f"{r['coef_shipped']:+.{d}f} ({r['se_shipped']:.{d}f})",
            "With full season FE": f"{r['coef_season_fe']:+.{d}f} ({r['se_season_fe']:.{d}f})",
            "Collinearity R²": f"{r['collinearity_r2']:.3f}",
        })
display(md(pd.DataFrame(rows)))
```

The collinearity that motivates excluding season fixed effects is overwhelming for the NFL (R²
= `{python} dot(pick(sfe, sport="nfl", outcome="home_win")["collinearity_r2"], 3)`) and strong for the NBA (`{python} dot(pick(sfe, sport="nba", outcome="home_win")["collinearity_r2"], 3)`). It is weaker for the NHL (`{python} dot(pick(sfe, sport="nhl", outcome="home_win")["collinearity_r2"], 3)`), and weaker still for
MLB (`{python} dot(pick(sfe, sport="mlb", outcome="home_win")["collinearity_r2"], 3)`, @tbl-sfe above). MLB's season-FE estimate keeps its sign and moves toward zero on
both outcomes, so weak collinearity there does not threaten the conclusion. The NHL's flips the
story. Under full season fixed effects the NHL win-probability estimate becomes
**`{python} sgn(pick(sfe, sport="nhl", outcome="home_win")["coef_season_fe"], 3)` (SE `{python} dot(pick(sfe, sport="nhl", outcome="home_win")["se_season_fe"], 3)`), the largest positive win-probability estimate in @tbl-sfe**, while the NFL's own season-FE win-probability estimate is `{python} sgn(pick(sfe, sport="nfl", outcome="home_win")["coef_season_fe"], 3)`, `{python} times(abs(pick(sfe, sport="nfl", outcome="home_win")["coef_season_fe"]) / pick(sfe, sport="nhl", outcome="home_win")["coef_season_fe"], 1)` larger
in magnitude. An analyst who preferred two-way fixed effects would report an NHL win-probability
estimate `{python} times(pick(sfe, sport="nhl", outcome="home_win")["coef_season_fe"] / pick(sfe, sport="nhl", outcome="home_win")["coef_shipped"], 1)` the shipped one, and at p = `{python} dot(pick(sfe, sport="nhl", outcome="home_win")["pvalue_season_fe"], 2)` on an interval that
still spans zero (`{python} civ(pick(sfe, sport="nhl", outcome="home_win")["ci_low_season_fe"], pick(sfe, sport="nhl", outcome="home_win")["ci_high_season_fe"], 3)`) would not be able to call it significant either. The NFL's two-way win-probability estimate,
`{python} sgn(lg_nfl_sfe_win["coef_season_fe"], 3)` (`{python} civ(lg_nfl_sfe_win["ci_low_season_fe"], lg_nfl_sfe_win["ci_high_season_fe"], 3)`, p = `{python} dot(lg_nfl_sfe_win["pvalue_season_fe"], 3)`), does
exclude zero, on the wrong side.

We think the shipped specification is still right, and the argument goes beyond collinearity. Within a *normal* season, crowd variation is demand-driven: good teams draw crowds and good
teams win. A season-fixed-effects specification identifies the crowd effect off exactly that
endogenous within-season variation. The within-season fits are consistent with that concern but
cannot confirm it. On win probability, within-2022 dose returns **`{python} sgn(lg_nhl_within2022_win, 3)`**, in a season whose
variation is mostly demand but includes Omicron-era caps on Canadian teams, while within-2021,
where variation was set largely by public-health policy, returns **`{python} sgn(pick(within, sport="nhl", outcome="home_win")["coef"], 2)`**. Neither fit is
distinguishable from zero.

**The NHL's within-season dose curve is wrong-signed.**

```{python}
#| label: tbl-within
#| tbl-cap: "Within-treated-season dose regressions, team fixed effects, no trend; MLB, with two treated seasons, also includes a treated-season dummy."
#| output: asis
rows = []
for s in SPORTS:  # B.S C-2: every league, not a selection
    for oc, lab, d in [("home_margin", "Margin", 3), ("home_win", "Win prob.", 3)]:
        r = pick(within, sport=s, outcome=oc)
        rows.append({
            "League": UP[s], "Outcome": lab,
            "Within-treated-season coef (SE)": f"{r['coef']:+.{d}f} ({r['se']:.{d}f})",
            "95% CI": ci(r["ci_low"], r["ci_high"], d),
            "p": f"{r['pvalue']:.3f}",
            "Raw mean, empty games": f"{r['raw_empty_mean']:+.3f} (n={int(r['n_empty'])})",
            "Raw mean, with fans": f"{r['raw_fans_mean']:+.3f} (n={int(r['n_fans'])})",
        })
display(md(pd.DataFrame(rows)))
# prose says only the NHL reverses its raw gap on BOTH outcomes (NFL win reverses alone).
_rev = within.assign(_r=(within["raw_fans_mean"] - within["raw_empty_mean"]) * within["coef"] < 0)
assert set(_rev.groupby("sport")["_r"].all().loc[lambda x: x].index) == {"nhl"}, "reword 'Only the NHL reverses on both outcomes'"
assert set(_rev.loc[_rev["_r"] & (_rev["sport"] == "nfl"), "outcome"]) == {"home_win"}, "reword the NFL win-reversal clause"
# the prose below says the NHL margin CI excludes zero on the wrong side and is the only
# within-season fit below p = .05; break loudly if the data stop saying so.
_wnm = pick(within, sport="nhl", outcome="home_margin")
within_n_sig = int((within["pvalue"] < 0.05).sum())
assert _wnm["ci_high"] < 0 and within_n_sig == 1, "reword the M5 clause in @sec-nhl"
```

The NHL's within-2021 margin coefficient of `{python} sgn(pick(within, sport="nhl", outcome="home_margin")["coef"], 2)` in @tbl-within
points the wrong way: more fans, worse home performance. Two caveats travel
with it permanently. First, within-team fan access in 2021 is confounded with calendar time,
because reopening was progressive, so "more fans" is very nearly "later in the season". Second, the
fitted support runs 0 to `{python} num(pick(within, sport="nhl", outcome="home_margin")["crowd_max"], 3)` with a 99th percentile of `{python} num(pick(within, sport="nhl", outcome="home_margin")["crowd_p99"], 3)`, so a per-unit coefficient
**extrapolates about `{python} times(1 / pick(within, sport="nhl", outcome="home_margin")["crowd_max"], 1)` beyond the data**.
Its team-clustered 95% interval, `{python} civ(_wnm["ci_low"], _wnm["ci_high"], 2)` (p = `{python} dot(_wnm["pvalue"])`),
excludes zero on the wrong side, and it is the only one of the `{python} words(len(within))` within-season fits
to clear p < .05. We do not read it as evidence that fans hurt home teams. The fits share data
and are not independent tests; the NHL win-probability fit points the same way but at
p = `{python} dot(pick(within, sport="nhl", outcome="home_win")["pvalue"])`; and the first caveat
applies directly, since the coefficient cannot separate more fans from later in the season.

The instructive part is the sign opposition in the NHL. The raw means go the *other* way there
(empty games `{python} sgn(pick(within, sport="nhl", outcome="home_margin")["raw_empty_mean"], 3)` against `{python} sgn(pick(within, sport="nhl", outcome="home_margin")["raw_fans_mean"], 3)` with fans, a gap of `{python} sgn(pick(within, sport="nhl", outcome="home_margin")["raw_fans_mean"] - pick(within, sport="nhl", outcome="home_margin")["raw_empty_mean"], 3)` goals), and
the team-fixed-effects coefficient reverses it. MLB's raw margin gap runs the same direction but is
only `{python} sgn(pick(within, sport="mlb", outcome="home_margin")["raw_fans_mean"] - pick(within, sport="mlb", outcome="home_margin")["raw_empty_mean"], 4)` runs, indistinguishable from no gap at all, and MLB's raw win-probability means do not reverse
at all: `{python} num(pick(within, sport="mlb", outcome="home_win")["raw_empty_mean"], 3)` empty against `{python} num(pick(within, sport="mlb", outcome="home_win")["raw_fans_mean"], 3)` with fans, the same direction as the negative coefficient. The NFL's win-probability fit also reverses its raw
gap, but its interval (`{python} civ(pick(within, sport="nfl", outcome="home_win")["ci_low"], pick(within, sport="nfl", outcome="home_win")["ci_high"], 2)`) is too wide to read. Only the NHL reverses on both
outcomes; we note the MLB sign agreement in passing but do not lean on it. The reversal is consistent with within-season crowd variation being confounded with which teams
reopened first and, within a team, with calendar time, which is why the headline estimate is
identified between seasons rather than within them.

## MLB: an identification problem before a power problem {#sec-mlb}

```{python}
#| label: leagues-mlb-vars
#| include: false
lg_mlb_margin = pick(twfe_all, sport="mlb", outcome="home_margin", sample="pooled")
lg_mlb_win = pick(twfe_all, sport="mlb", outcome="home_win", sample="pooled")
lg_mlb_overlap_all = pick(overlap, sport="mlb", scope="all_treated")["control_overlap"]
lg_mlb_overlap_2020 = pick(overlap, sport="mlb", scope="2020")["control_overlap"]
lg_mlb_overlap_2021 = pick(overlap, sport="mlb", scope="2021")["control_overlap"]
lg_mlb_dose_2021 = pick(overlap, sport="mlb", scope="2021")["treated_mean"]
lg_mlb_mde_unscaled_margin, lg_mlb_mde_rescaled_margin = _mde_ratios("mlb", "home_margin")
lg_mlb_desc = pick(desc, sport="mlb", season="pooled_fullcrowd")
# estimator (b)'s MLB intervals, pooled sample, both outcomes.
lg_mlb_did_margin = pick(did_all, sport="mlb", outcome="home_margin", sample="pooled")
lg_mlb_did_win = pick(did_all, sport="mlb", outcome="home_win", sample="pooled")
assert lg_mlb_did_margin["ci_low"] < 0 < lg_mlb_did_margin["ci_high"] and lg_mlb_did_win["ci_low"] < 0 < lg_mlb_did_win["ci_high"], \
    "estimator (b) MLB interval no longer spans zero; reword @sec-mlb part (1)"
```

MLB is the one league whose null needs a different explanation, and the explanation is mainly
about identification. It has four parts.

**(1) The estimate is indistinguishable from zero, not a reversal.** MLB's margin coefficient is `{python} sgn(lg_mlb_margin["coef"], 2)`
with a 95% interval of `{python} civ(lg_mlb_margin["ci_low"], lg_mlb_margin["ci_high"], 3)` (p = `{python} dot(lg_mlb_margin["pvalue"], 3)`), and its win-probability coefficient is `{python} sgn(lg_mlb_win["coef"], 3)`,
interval `{python} civ(lg_mlb_win["ci_low"], lg_mlb_win["ci_high"], 3)` (p = `{python} dot(lg_mlb_win["pvalue"], 3)`). Estimator (b) gives
`{python} civ(lg_mlb_did_margin["ci_low"], lg_mlb_did_margin["ci_high"], 3)` (p = `{python} dot(lg_mlb_did_margin["pvalue"], 3)`) on margin and
`{python} civ(lg_mlb_did_win["ci_low"], lg_mlb_did_win["ci_high"], 3)` (p = `{python} dot(lg_mlb_did_win["pvalue"], 3)`) on win probability. The negative
sign is indistinguishable from noise. Nothing in this study supports
the sentence "empty stadiums helped MLB home teams".

**(2) The natural experiment barely applies to baseball.** From @tbl-dose: **`{python} pct(lg_mlb_overlap_all, 1)` of MLB's
control-season games fall inside the treated seasons' dose range**, against under 0.6% for the
other `{python} words(len(SPORTS) - 1)` leagues. For the NFL, NBA and NHL, the treatment is a near-disjoint empty-versus-full
contrast. For MLB it is closer to an extension of ordinary demand
variation, and MLB's coefficient rides partly on that ordinary variation, which is exactly
the endogenous channel the design exists to avoid.

The contamination is entirely 2021. MLB's 2020 season overlaps the control distribution `{python} pct(lg_mlb_overlap_2020, 2)` of
the time, no more than the NFL's, while 2021 overlaps `{python} pct(lg_mlb_overlap_2021, 1)` at a mean dose of `{python} num(lg_mlb_dose_2021, 3)`. The obvious
move is to define MLB's treatment as 2020 only. **We do not**: the paper keeps the 2020+2021
definition throughout, because the trade runs in both directions. 2020 buys dose cleanliness and
pays for it in confounding. The 60-game 2020 season introduced the extra-innings ghost runner, the
universal designated hitter, seven-inning doubleheaders and a regionalized schedule, several of
which push home advantage in the home team's direction and none of which is a crowd effect. 2021
buys a clean, full-length season and pays for it in the dose overlap documented above. **No MLB
definition is clean on both margins.**

```{python}
#| label: tbl-mlbsplit
#| tbl-cap: "MLB treated-season split. **The sign convention here is not the paper's elsewhere**: these are raw treated-year level indicators, unnegated, so a *positive* value implies a *negative* crowd effect. Both years enter one regression (n = 12,871); each absorbs the other if omitted."
#| output: asis
rows = []
for oc, lab, d in [("home_margin", "Margin", 4), ("home_win", "Win prob.", 4)]:
    r = {"Outcome": lab}
    for y in [2020, 2021]:
        x = pick(mlbsplit, outcome=oc, treated_year=y)
        r[str(y)] = f"{x['coef']:+.{d}f} ({x['se']:.{d}f}), p={x['pvalue']:.2f}"
    rows.append(r)
display(md(pd.DataFrame(rows)))
```

The split does not resolve the question. Both treated years come out slightly positive on the
year-indicator level, all with p > .29, which **does not confirm** a 2020-rule-artifact story,
and could not have separated rule changes from crowd effects even had it come out cleanly. We
report it as inconclusive because that is what it is.

**(3) Run margin is the noisiest outcome in the study relative to its own effect.** MLB's
minimum detectable effect on margin is `{python} times(lg_mlb_mde_unscaled_margin, 1)` its entire home advantage at per-unit scaling (`{python} times(lg_mlb_mde_rescaled_margin, 1)`
rescaled), the worst cell in @tbl-mde by a wide margin. Baseball's descriptive margin home
advantage is `{python} sgn(lg_mlb_desc["mean_home_margin"], 3)` runs with a standard error of `{python} num(lg_mlb_desc["home_margin_se"], 3)`. There is essentially no signal there to
detect.

**(4) Baseball's known home-advantage mechanisms are largely crowd-independent.** The home team
bats last; that survives an empty stadium untouched. Park familiarity survives it too: the
particular carry of the air, the dimensions, the mound, the sightlines from the box. The channel
through which the published literature most credibly links crowds to outcomes is officiating bias
under crowd pressure [@leitner2021referees; @plosone_nhl_penalties]. Home-plate umpires do favor
the home side on called pitches [@flannagan2024umpire], and one recent study finds that this bias
rises with ballpark occupancy and is indistinguishable from zero in the fan-free 2020 season
[@saiegh2026umpire]. But that bias is worth hundredths of a run per game, its implied effect on win
probability is small and imprecisely estimated, and peer-reviewed studies of 2020 find no
significant change in overall home advantage [@losak2021baseball; @chiu2022mlb]. Baseball's total home advantage is also the smallest of the
`{python} words(len(SPORTS))` leagues studied here on win percentage. A league whose home advantage is small, whose known mechanisms are
mostly crowd-independent, and whose outcome measure is the noisiest, is the league where a null
was least surprising.

The claim we can defend for baseball is **"no detectable MLB crowd effect."** The claim we cannot
defend, and do not make, is "crowds do not matter in baseball."

# Robustness and sensitivity {#sec-robust}

## The restricted sample

Estimator (a) was also refitted on a restricted sample, the treated season(s) plus their
immediate neighbors, as a check on whether distant control seasons were driving the result
(estimator (b)'s restricted-sample values are in `did_*.csv`).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-restricted
#| tbl-cap: "Pooled versus restricted estimation windows."
#| output: asis
from src.models.twfe import _restricted_seasons
rows = []
_se_ratio = []
_away_cells = []
rob_collapse_count = 0
for s in SPORTS:
    for oc, lab, d in [("home_margin", "Margin", 3), ("home_win", "Win prob.", 4)]:
        p = pick(twfe_all, sport=s, outcome=oc, sample="pooled")
        r = pick(twfe_all, sport=s, outcome=oc, sample="restricted")
        rows.append({
            "League": UP[s], "Outcome": lab,
            "Pooled": f"{p['coef']:+.{d}f} ({p['se']:.{d}f})",
            "Restricted": f"{r['coef']:+.{d}f} ({r['se']:.{d}f})",
            "n pooled": int(p["n_obs"]), "n restricted": int(r["n_obs"]),
        })
        if abs(r["coef"]) < abs(p["coef"]):
            rob_collapse_count += 1
        else:
            _away_cells.append((s, oc))
        _se_ratio.append(r["se"] / p["se"] - 1)
        if s == "nfl" and oc == "home_margin":
            rob_restricted_nfl_margin = r["coef"]
rob_n_cells = len(SPORTS) * 2
rob_se_ratio_min, rob_se_ratio_max = min(_se_ratio), max(_se_ratio)
# the one cell that moves away from zero on the restricted
# window is no longer NHL margin (which now moves toward zero) but NBA win probability. Name it
# live instead of hardcoding which cell it is.
assert _away_cells == [("nba", "home_win")], \
    "the restricted-window 'moves away from zero' cell is no longer NBA win probability; reword @sec-robust and @tbl-specsummary"
rob_away_cell_label = f"{UP[_away_cells[0][0]]} {_LAB[_away_cells[0][1]]}"
rob_ctrl_kept_share = {}
for s in SPORTS:
    d = _prep(pd.read_parquet(ROOT / "data" / "processed" / f"{s}.parquet"))
    ctrl = d[~d["season"].isin(TREATED[s])]
    kept = ctrl[ctrl["season"].isin(_restricted_seasons(TREATED[s]))]
    rob_ctrl_kept_share[s] = len(kept) / len(ctrl)
assert max(rob_ctrl_kept_share.values()) < 0.5, \
    "restricted window keeps >=half the control games in some league; reword @sec-robust"
display(md(pd.DataFrame(rows)))
```

On the restricted window
`{python} words(rob_collapse_count)` of `{python} words(rob_n_cells)` estimates move toward zero,
and the NFL's margin estimate falls from `{python} sgn(strat_nfl_coef_shipped, 2)` to `{python} sgn(rob_restricted_nfl_margin, 2)`; `{python} rob_away_cell_label`
is the one that moves away from zero. Two readings are available and we cannot adjudicate between
them with these data. Either the pooled estimates are being carried by distant control seasons
(for the NFL, @sec-loso shows this is partly true of 2018 specifically), or the restricted window
discards most of the control mass and most of the leverage the linear trend needs, leaving a
noisier estimate that has drifted toward zero. The standard errors do not separate these: they move by only `{python} pct(rob_se_ratio_min, 1)`–`{python} pct(rob_se_ratio_max, 1)`
despite the restricted window discarding more than half the control games in every league,
consistent with the treated season's own sampling error dominating either way (cf. @sec-floor).

What we can say is that the restricted-sample result is consistent with the paper's thesis under
either reading: this design does not have the resolution to distinguish these hypotheses.

## The betting spread is a bad control, not a fragility test

```{python}
#| label: rob-spread-vars
#| include: false
_nfl_raw = pd.read_parquet(ROOT / "data" / "processed" / "nfl.parquet")
_rob_spread_margin = fit(_nfl_raw, "home_margin", "pooled", TREATED["nfl"], extra_controls=["closing_spread"])
_rob_spread_win = fit(_nfl_raw, "home_win", "pooled", TREATED["nfl"], extra_controls=["closing_spread"])
rob_spread_margin_coef = _rob_spread_margin["coef"]
rob_spread_margin_se = _rob_spread_margin["se"]
rob_spread_win_coef = _rob_spread_win["coef"]
```

Adding the NFL closing spread as a control attenuates the margin coefficient from `{python} sgn(strat_nfl_coef_shipped, 2)` to
**`{python} sgn(rob_spread_margin_coef, 2)`** (SE `{python} num(rob_spread_margin_se, 2)`) and the win-probability coefficient from `{python} sgn(res_nfl_winprob_pp / 100, 3)` to `{python} sgn(rob_spread_win_coef, 3)`. A naive reading is
that the crowd effect does not survive controlling for market expectations.

That reading is wrong, and the reason is a textbook one. **The closing spread is post-treatment.**
It is set by a market that knows the stadium will be empty and has already priced in a reduced
home advantage. Conditioning on it is conditioning on a variable that contains the treatment
effect, absorbing at least part of the quantity we are estimating, so the attenuation cannot be
read as evidence against it. The spread is reported here as a diagnostic and is excluded from the main
specification for that reason. It is also NFL-only, so it could never have been a sport-blind
main-model control.

## The playoff exclusion, and descriptive playoff home advantage {#sec-playoffs}

Playoffs are excluded from every model in this paper. In the NFL the higher seed hosts every
playoff game before the neutral-site Super Bowl; in the NBA, NHL and MLB it hosts the first game
of every series and any deciding game, and every game of MLB's post-2022 Wild Card round. Playoff home advantage therefore bundles the
crowd, travel and familiarity channels with a seeding asymmetry, and seeding tracks team quality
in a way regular-season home advantage does not. Adding playoff games would change measured
home advantage for reasons unrelated to crowds, without adding identification.

For completeness, the descriptive playoff picture:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-playoff
#| tbl-cap: "Descriptive playoff home advantage, computed inline. Seasons with no clean playoff games are absent rather than reported as zero-game rows: the NBA's and NHL's 2020 postseasons were played entirely in bubbles and are excluded in full. These numbers blend home advantage with seeding quality and should be read with that caveat."
#| output: asis
from src.viz.descriptive import summarize
rows = []
for s in SPORTS:
    p = pd.read_parquet(ROOT / "data" / "processed" / f"{s}.parquet")
    t = summarize(p, playoffs=True)
    full = t[t["season"] == "pooled_fullcrowd"].iloc[0]
    per = t[t["season"] != "pooled_fullcrowd"]
    tr = per[per["covid_era"]]
    rows.append({
        "League": UP[s],
        "n (full-crowd playoffs)": int(full["n_games"]),
        "Playoff home win %": f"{full['home_win_pct']:.3f} ({full['home_win_se']:.3f})",
        "Playoff home margin": f"{full['mean_home_margin']:+.3f} ({full['home_margin_se']:.3f})",
        "Regular-season home win %": f"{pick(desc, sport=s, season='pooled_fullcrowd')['home_win_pct']:.3f}",
        "Restricted-season playoff win %": " / ".join(f"{v:.3f}" for v in tr["home_win_pct"]) or "—",
    })
    _reg_win = pick(desc, sport=s, season="pooled_fullcrowd")["home_win_pct"]
    if s == "nfl":
        rob_playoff_nfl_win, rob_playoff_nfl_reg_win = full["home_win_pct"], _reg_win
    elif s == "nba":
        rob_playoff_nba_win, rob_playoff_nba_reg_win = full["home_win_pct"], _reg_win
    elif s == "nhl":
        rob_playoff_nhl_win, rob_playoff_nhl_reg_win = full["home_win_pct"], _reg_win
    elif s == "mlb":
        rob_playoff_mlb_win, rob_playoff_mlb_margin, rob_playoff_mlb_n = \
            full["home_win_pct"], full["mean_home_margin"], full["n_games"]
        rob_playoff_mlb_win_se, rob_playoff_mlb_reg_win = full["home_win_se"], _reg_win
assert abs(rob_playoff_mlb_win - 0.5) / rob_playoff_mlb_win_se < 1.96, \
    "MLB playoff win % no longer within sampling noise of .500; reword @sec-playoffs"
assert abs(rob_playoff_mlb_win - rob_playoff_mlb_reg_win) / rob_playoff_mlb_win_se < 1.96, \
    "MLB playoff win % no longer within sampling noise of the regular-season rate; reword @sec-playoffs"
display(md(pd.DataFrame(rows)))
```

Playoff home advantage is larger than regular-season home advantage in the NFL (`{python} dot(rob_playoff_nfl_win)` versus `{python} dot(rob_playoff_nfl_reg_win)`)
and the NBA (`{python} dot(rob_playoff_nba_win)` versus `{python} dot(rob_playoff_nba_reg_win)`), marginally *lower* in the NHL (`{python} dot(rob_playoff_nhl_win)` versus `{python} dot(rob_playoff_nhl_reg_win)`), and
*inverted* in MLB, where the home team wins `{python} pct(rob_playoff_mlb_win, 1)` of clean playoff games and concedes `{python} num(abs(rob_playoff_mlb_margin), 2)` runs
per game on average across `{python} thou(rob_playoff_mlb_n)` games, a gap that is within sampling noise of both .500 and the
regular-season rate. We resist the temptation to read anything causal into it.
The seeding asymmetry that may inflate the NFL and NBA numbers is present in baseball too; the
samples are small; and MLB's playoff format changed within the window. It is reported because
excluding a slice of data obliges one to show what was excluded.

## Zero-attendance reporting artifacts {#sec-zero}

```{python}
#| label: rob-zero-vars
#| include: false
_z = zsens.assign(shift_se=(zsens["coef_post"] - zsens["coef_pre"]).abs() / zsens["se_post"])
_zmax = _z.loc[_z["shift_se"].idxmax()]
rob_zero_max_shift_se = _zmax["shift_se"]
rob_zero_max_label = f"{UP[_zmax['sport']]} {_LAB[_zmax['outcome']]}"
rob_zero_max_pre, rob_zero_max_post = _zmax["coef_pre"], _zmax["coef_post"]
rob_zero_dp = 2 if _zmax["outcome"] == "home_margin" else 3

def _excl_set(tw, ov):
    out = set()
    for s in SPORTS:
        for oc in ("home_margin", "home_win"):
            r = tw[(tw["sport"] == s) & (tw["outcome"] == oc) & (tw["sample"] == "pooled")].iloc[0]
            cm = ov[(ov["sport"] == s) & (ov["scope"] == "all_treated")]["control_mean"].iloc[0]
            h = _intro_hfa[s][oc]
            if all(r["ci_high"] < x or r["ci_low"] > x for x in (h, h / cm)):
                out.add((s, oc))
    return out

_pre = T / "pre_zero_fix"
_excl_pre = _excl_set(pd.concat([pd.read_csv(_pre / f"twfe_{s}.csv") for s in SPORTS]),
                      pd.read_csv(_pre / "dose_overlap.csv"))

# Baseline for the zero-artifact fix's OWN effect is "before the reopening-zeros fix" on both
# sides (pre_zero_fix vs pre_reopen_fix), not vs. today's fully-corrected _excl_cells — the
# reopening fix (below) is a second, later correction that moves this set on its own.
_pre_reopen = T / "pre_reopen_fix"
_excl_pre_reopen = _excl_set(pd.concat([pd.read_csv(_pre_reopen / f"twfe_{s}.csv") for s in SPORTS]),
                             pd.read_csv(_pre_reopen / "dose_overlap.csv"))
assert _excl_pre == _excl_pre_reopen, "full-advantage exclusion cells differ pre/post zero-artifact correction; reword @sec-zero"
rob_zero_excl_count = len(_excl_pre_reopen)
# the prose names these cells.
assert _excl_pre_reopen == {("mlb", "home_win"), ("nba", "home_win"), ("nhl", "home_margin")}, \
    "pre-reopen exclusion cells no longer MLB win, NBA win, NHL margin; reword @sec-zero"
```

Coding the `{python} thou(data_zero_nulled_total)` zero-attendance reports as empty stadiums instead, as every estimate did before
the correction, moves no pooled dose-response coefficient by more than `{python} num(rob_zero_max_shift_se, 2)` of its standard
error. The largest move is `{python} rob_zero_max_label` (`{python} sgn(rob_zero_max_post, rob_zero_dp)` with the zeros as missing, `{python} sgn(rob_zero_max_pre, rob_zero_dp)` with them as empty), and the same `{python} words(rob_zero_excl_count)` cells
(MLB win probability, NBA win probability, NHL margin) exclude a full-advantage effect either way (both before the reopening-zeros correction below). Both versions are in `zero_attendance_sensitivity.csv`.

The two NHL teams introduced in @sec-dose, Nashville and St. Louis, are also this fix's weakest
evidence, and it is worth saying plainly where that evidence sits relative to the numbers. Restoring
their `{python} rob_reopen_nsh_stl_n`
zeros to real moves NHL by `{python} num(rob_reopen_nsh_stl_dmargin, 3)` on margin and `{python} num(rob_reopen_nsh_stl_dwin, 3)`
on win probability, and does not restore the dropped NHL-margin exclusion either way. The NBA headline
shift is the opposite case: restoring `{python} rob_reopen_nba_best_n` games from Miami, Indiana and
Sacramento (the three teams with a named, dated local-news source) returns NBA win probability to
`{python} sgn(rob_reopen_nba_best_restored_win, 4)`, essentially the entire shift this correction produced.
The fix's weakest evidence is therefore immaterial to every estimate, and its strongest evidence is
what moved the numbers.

Detroit's sourced first-fans date is kept at 2021-03-10 even though one fan account describes earlier
public attendance in January 2021; crediting that account would reclassify 12 more games. And the
audit did not exhaustively check whether a nonzero ESPN attendance figure from a family- or
staff-only game could set a first-fans date too early for some team.

## Trend specification {#sec-trend}

```{python}
#| label: rob-trend-spec-vars
#| include: false
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
rob_trend_nfl_win_quad = pick(trend, sport="nfl", outcome="home_win", trend="quadratic")["coef"]
rob_trend_nfl_margin_quad = pick(trend, sport="nfl", outcome="home_margin", trend="quadratic")["coef"]
rob_trend_nba_win_quad = pick(trend, sport="nba", outcome="home_win", trend="quadratic")["coef"]
rob_trend_mlb_win_quad = pick(trend, sport="mlb", outcome="home_win", trend="quadratic")["coef"]
rob_trend_mlb_win_quad_dse = (
    (rob_trend_mlb_win_quad - pick(trend, sport="mlb", outcome="home_win", trend="linear")["coef"])
    / pick(trend, sport="mlb", outcome="home_win", trend="linear")["se"])
rob_quadr2 = {}
for s in SPORTS:
    _p = pd.read_parquet(ROOT / "data" / "processed" / f"{s}.parquet")
    _d = _prep(_p)[["crowd_pct", "season", "home_team"]].dropna().copy()
    _d["t"] = _d["season"] - _d["season"].min()
    rob_quadr2[s] = smf.ols("crowd_pct ~ C(home_team) + t + I(t**2)", data=_d).fit().rsquared
assert rob_quadr2["nfl"] < strat_r2_nfl - 0.5, \
    "NFL quadratic-trend R² no longer clearly below the season-FE R²; reword @sec-robust"

# C1 fix: the quadratic trend is not a second, independent fragility -- it reproduces the
# drop-2018 result (@sec-loso). Check live: with 2018 dropped, does the quadratic still move
# either NFL outcome by much relative to the linear-trend/drop-2018 fit?
_nfl_drop2018 = _nfl_raw[_nfl_raw["season"] != 2018]
rob_trend_drop2018_max = max(
    abs(fit(_nfl_drop2018, oc, "pooled", TREATED["nfl"], trend="quadratic")["coef"]
        - fit(_nfl_drop2018, oc, "pooled", TREATED["nfl"], trend="linear")["coef"])
    / fit(_nfl_drop2018, oc, "pooled", TREATED["nfl"], trend="linear")["se"]
    for oc in ("home_margin", "home_win"))
assert rob_trend_drop2018_max < 0.25, \
    "quadratic no longer close to the drop-2018 linear result; reword @sec-trend"
```

A quadratic season trend moves the study's largest estimate. Under it
the NFL win-probability estimate goes from `{python} sgn(res_nfl_winprob_pp / 100, 3)` to `{python} sgn(rob_trend_nfl_win_quad, 3)`
and the margin estimate from `{python} sgn(strat_nfl_coef_shipped, 2)` to `{python} sgn(rob_trend_nfl_margin_quad, 2)`, and NBA win
probability falls to about zero (`{python} sgn(rob_trend_nba_win_quad, 4)`); MLB win probability moves
`{python} sgn(rob_trend_mlb_win_quad_dse, 2)` SE (`{python} sgn(lg_mlb_win["coef"], 3)` → `{python} sgn(rob_trend_mlb_win_quad, 3)`). Unlike full season fixed effects, a quadratic
trend is not near-collinear with the dose (R² of `crowd_pct` on team fixed effects and a quadratic
trend: NFL `{python} dot(rob_quadr2["nfl"])`, versus `{python} dot(strat_r2_nfl)` with full season dummies), so this cannot be
dismissed the same way. This is the same fragility as @sec-loso's 2018 result, seen through the
trend rather than the sample: with 2018 dropped, the quadratic moves neither NFL estimate by more
than `{python} num(rob_trend_drop2018_max, 2)` SE.

| Choice | Alternative tested | Effect on the headline |
|---|---|---|
| Linear season trend | None; quadratic | Small with no trend (≤`{python} num(rob_trend_none_max, 2)` SE, every league); a quadratic moves NFL win `{python} sgn(rob_trend_nfl_win_quad_dse, 2)` SE (`{python} sgn(res_nfl_winprob_pp / 100, 3)` → `{python} sgn(rob_trend_nfl_win_quad, 3)`) and NFL margin `{python} sgn(rob_trend_nfl_margin_quad_dse, 2)` SE (@tbl-trend for the NHL; @sec-trend) |
| Team FE only | Two-way (full season FE) | Signs flip in the NFL and NBA; NHL grows, MLB shrinks toward zero; NFL margin `{python} sgn(strat_nfl_coef_shipped, 2)` → `{python} sgn(strat_nfl_coef_seasonfe, 2)` (@tbl-sfe) |
| Pooled window | Treated ± adjacent seasons | `{python} words(rob_collapse_count).capitalize()` of `{python} words(rob_n_cells)` move toward zero; `{python} rob_away_cell_label` moves away from zero (@tbl-restricted) |
| `{python} words(intro_n_seasons).capitalize()`-season panel | Drop each untreated season | NFL−2018 win `{python} sgn(lg_loso_nfl_2018_win_delta_se, 2)` SE (margin `{python} sgn(rob_loso_nfl_2018_margin_dse, 2)` SE) (@tbl-loso); NBA win flips sign dropping 2023 (`{python} sgn(rob_loso_nba_2023_win_dse, 2)` SE) (@sec-loso; `leave_one_season_out.csv`) |
| Controls: Elo, rest, travel | Drop travel (NHL) | `{python} sgn(rob_travel_delta_win, 4)` win probability, same n |
| No spread control | Add NFL closing spread | `{python} sgn(strat_nfl_coef_shipped, 2)` → `{python} sgn(rob_spread_margin_coef, 2)`, and post-treatment by construction |
| Between-season identification | Within-treated-season dose | NHL: wrong-signed, extrapolating `{python} times(rob_within_nhl_extrap, 1)` beyond support (@tbl-within) |
| Zero attendance outside restriction windows as missing | Coded as empty (0) | ≤ `{python} num(rob_zero_max_shift_se, 2)` SE in every cell (@sec-zero) |
| Zeros after a team readmitted fans as missing | Coded as empty (0) | ≤ `{python} num(rob_reopen_max_shift_se, 2)` SE in every cell (@sec-zero) |
