# Relation to the published literature {#sec-lit}

## What prior work found

The ghost-game literature is **predominantly, but not unanimously, in favor of a crowd effect on
match results**. A systematic review of 26 primary studies of football (20
peer-reviewed) reports a vote count of six finding no change, two a slightly
reduced home advantage, eight a reduced home advantage and ten a strongly reduced home advantage,
with "not a single study that found an *increased* home advantage in ghost games"
[@systematicreview_ghostgames]. A separate review of 28 articles splits its sample by outcome type
rather than by direction and records dissenting match-outcome findings, including a Brazilian
analysis finding *fewer* home wins in the spectator-attended 2019 season than in the
spectator-free 2020 [@wang2023crowdreview].

Three nulls, one of them (Schank's) an unrefereed working paper, deserve naming.
@schank2024bundesliga, which the authors describe as the first study to cover all three
regulated Bundesliga seasons, finds home advantage in the near-complete spectator-ban season
2020/21 "very close to" the pre-COVID 2018/19 season, although it vanished in the 2019/20 ghost
games. The same study finds a non-monotone dose relationship in 2021/22 (the authors call it
U-shaped), with the largest home advantage at *medium* stadium utilization. @higgs2021nba report no
meaningful MLB change. @gong2022nbafouls finds no crowd effect on NBA referee home bias in clutch
time across 1,679 games and 30,695 plays.

A commonly cited channel in American football, crowd noise drowning out the visiting offense's
snap count, has been tested on NFL play-by-play for 2018–2020.
@farnell2023nflpenalties finds that "crowds play no role in an offense committing penalties at the
line of scrimmage, neither for the home nor the away team." The crowd effect it does find runs
through the other side of the ball: home defenses commit fewer pre-snap penalties when stadiums are
full, which the author reads as noise drowning out the visiting quarterback's cadence. The author
also notes that other COVID-era changes, such as altered practice regimes, could produce the same
pattern. From 1989 until 2007 the NFL enforced a rule that let referees penalize teams for crowd
noise [@farnell2023nflpenalties, n. 2].

In college football, @mcmahon2024cfb find that larger crowds lowered away-team scoring before 2020
and attribute this to noise, because the association is no longer significant in 2020, when
stadiums were allowed to pipe in artificial crowd noise. Their 2020 estimate is larger in magnitude
but far less precise, so the evidence is a loss of significance rather than a measured decline, and
the authors themselves caution against reading it too strongly as causal. In baseball,
@saiegh2026umpire find that home-favoring umpire bias rises with ballpark occupancy and is
indistinguishable from zero in the fan-free 2020 season, though the bias is worth only hundredths
of a run per game. Those authors decline to read their own instrumented estimate as causal, and we
do not read it that way either.

The effect sizes also show a pattern that bears on our own window: **the strongest
reductions are concentrated in the first, short, dramatic ghost-game window** (the last nine
Bundesliga matchdays of 2019/20, the European ghost games of spring 2020). Longer-window results
are weaker, which @schank2024bundesliga reads as teams becoming accustomed to empty stadiums. Our
estimation window is at least one *full* restricted season per league, which is the longer-window case.

## Where our estimates sit

```{python}
#| label: lit-nba-vars
#| include: false
from src.models.twfe import _prep
_lit_nba_clean = _prep(_nba_raw)
lit_nba_margin = pick(twfe_all, sport="nba", outcome="home_margin", sample="pooled")

_lit_nba_ov = pick(overlap, sport="nba", scope="all_treated")
lit_nba_control_mean = _lit_nba_ov["control_mean"]
lit_nba_treated_mean = _lit_nba_ov["treated_mean"]
lit_nba_dose_gap = lit_nba_control_mean - lit_nba_treated_mean
lit_nba_zero_share = _lit_nba_ov["treated_share_zero"]

# Q9 fix: Ganz & Allsop's 1.69 is a raw within-2020-21 fans-vs-no-fans gap, not a causal
# estimate in our units. Their own evidence (categorical fan-count bins) reads as a presence
# effect rather than a size effect (primary source pp. 37, 41-43), so we map their uninstrumented
# any-fans-present FE estimate through our dose data via presence share, not raw dose.
GANZ_FE_PRESENCE, GANZ_FE_PRESENCE_SE = 4.527, 2.074
_lnc = _lit_nba_clean.dropna(subset=["crowd_pct", "home_margin"])
_lnc_treated = _lnc["season"].isin(TREATED["nba"])
lit_nba_presence_control = (_lnc.loc[~_lnc_treated, "crowd_pct"] > 0).mean()
lit_nba_presence_treated = (_lnc.loc[_lnc_treated, "crowd_pct"] > 0).mean()
_presence_gap = lit_nba_presence_control - lit_nba_presence_treated
lit_nba_implied = GANZ_FE_PRESENCE * _presence_gap / lit_nba_dose_gap
lit_nba_implied_ci_low = (GANZ_FE_PRESENCE - 1.96 * GANZ_FE_PRESENCE_SE) * _presence_gap / lit_nba_dose_gap
lit_nba_implied_ci_high = (GANZ_FE_PRESENCE + 1.96 * GANZ_FE_PRESENCE_SE) * _presence_gap / lit_nba_dose_gap
lit_nba_implied_ratio = lit_nba_margin["coef"] / lit_nba_implied

_lit_nba_margin_se = lit_nba_margin["se"]
def _lit_power(effect, se):
    z = effect / se
    return _phi(z - 1.96) + _phi(-z - 1.96)
lit_nba_implied_power = _lit_power(lit_nba_implied, _lit_nba_margin_se)

# N1: Ganz & Allsop drop IND/MIA/SAC for reporting zero after reopening; our pipeline nulls those
# artifact zeros instead (@sec-zero), and _lnc drops them. Counting the nulled 2021 games as
# fans-present is the other defensible reading, so report it beside the shipped one.
_lnc_all = _lit_nba_clean.dropna(subset=["home_margin"])
_lnc_all_treated = _lnc_all["season"].isin(TREATED["nba"])
_present_all = (_lnc_all["crowd_pct"] > 0) | _lnc_all["crowd_pct"].isna()
lit_nba_null_n = int(_lnc_all.loc[_lnc_all_treated, "crowd_pct"].isna().sum())
lit_nba_implied_nullpresent = GANZ_FE_PRESENCE * (
    _present_all[~_lnc_all_treated].mean() - _present_all[_lnc_all_treated].mean()) / lit_nba_dose_gap

_ci_lo, _ci_hi = lit_nba_margin["ci_low"], lit_nba_margin["ci_high"]
for _imp in (lit_nba_implied, lit_nba_implied_nullpresent):
    assert _ci_lo + 0.85 * (_ci_hi - _ci_lo) < _imp < _ci_hi, \
        "Ganz presence mapping left the upper edge of our NBA interval; reword @sec-lit, abstract, intro, conclusion"
    assert 0.28 < lit_nba_margin["coef"] / _imp < 0.38, \
        "our NBA estimate is no longer about a third of the Ganz mapping; reword @sec-lit and intro"
```

The closest comparison available is NBA points margin. @ganz2024nbafans report the
+2.13/+0.44 pair as raw average home-court-advantage points within the 2020–21 season, with fans
present and without; they describe the difference as only marginally significant (p = .09). (This
pair is sometimes attributed to @higgs2021nba, whose Bayesian negative-binomial model reports
home-advantage parameters on the log scale and contains no such figures; it is Ganz & Allsop's.)
Their regression estimates, instrumented with maximum allowable capacity, are +1.74 points per
additional 1,000 fans (SE 0.69) and, uninstrumented, +4.53 points for fans allowed against none
(SE 2.07); similar effects for arenas allowing 1–3,000 fans (4.3) and over 3,000 (5.1) point to
presence rather than size. No team was permitted even half of capacity in 2020–21.

Our descriptive NBA numbers are **`{python} sgn(desc_nba_margin_pooled, 2)` with fans and `{python} sgn(desc_nba_margin_treated, 2)` in the restricted season**, a raw drop
of `{python} num(desc_nba_margin_pooled - desc_nba_margin_treated, 2)` points, set beside their raw 1.69
(their 2020–21 difference, not a causal estimate). Their with- and without-fans figures both come
from 2020–21 games; ours compare normal seasons
against a restricted season that mixed empty and partial-crowd games (`{python} pct(lit_nba_zero_share, 1)` of treated
games at zero dose), so the two drops are not like-for-like. Our descriptive data are not
inconsistent with theirs. What differs is our *modeled* estimate:
`{python} sgn(lit_nba_margin["coef"], 2)` points per unit of crowd dose, with a 95% interval of
`{python} civ(lit_nba_margin["ci_low"], lit_nba_margin["ci_high"], 2)`.

Their units are not ours (fans present within a sparse 2020–21 crowd, against empty-to-full dose
across seasons), so 1.69 does not convert into our units directly. Their own evidence favors a
*presence* effect, so we map their +4.53 presence estimate through our dose data on that basis,
proxying fans allowed by fans attended: a presence effect moves a game only if any fans attended, true of `{python} pct(lit_nba_presence_control, 1)` of our
full-crowd-season NBA games and `{python} pct(lit_nba_presence_treated, 1)` of 2021 games, while
mean dose fell from `{python} num(lit_nba_control_mean, 2)` to `{python} num(lit_nba_treated_mean, 2)`.
The implied coefficient in our specification (`{python} num(GANZ_FE_PRESENCE, 3)` times the
control-minus-treated presence share, divided by the control-minus-treated dose) is
**`{python} sgn(lit_nba_implied, 2)`**, at the upper edge of our interval. Ganz & Allsop drop
Indiana, Miami and Sacramento for reporting zero attendance after their arenas reopened; we null
reporting zeros after reopening for every team, those three included (@sec-data), which drops the
games from this calculation. Counting
the `{python} lit_nba_null_n` nulled 2021 games as fans-present gives
`{python} sgn(lit_nba_implied_nullpresent, 2)`, still in the upper part of our interval. Their 95% interval
(`{python} num(GANZ_FE_PRESENCE, 3)` ± 1.96 × `{python} num(GANZ_FE_PRESENCE_SE, 3)`) maps the same
way to `{python} civ(lit_nba_implied_ci_low, lit_nba_implied_ci_high, 2)`, which overlaps ours; our
point estimate is about a third of theirs (`{python} pct(lit_nba_implied_ratio, 0)`). Our power to
detect `{python} num(lit_nba_implied, 2)` points, at our NBA margin standard error of
`{python} num(_lit_nba_margin_se, 4)`, is `{python} pct(lit_nba_implied_power, 0)`. Two assumptions
carry this mapping: that Ganz & Allsop's effect is one of presence rather than size, and that a
2020–21 crowd effect generalizes to full-crowd seasons.

No such mapping is attempted for the football studies (draws break the binary outcome and a 3-1-0
points system is not a win probability) nor for @higgs2021nba, whose log-scale parameters have no
published translation. Where a conversion cannot be made honestly, the comparison is left
unmade.

## Mechanism versus outcome: the NHL case

```{python}
#| label: lit-nhl-vars
#| include: false
lit_nhl_hfa = pick(noise, sport="nhl", outcome="home_margin")["hfa"]
lit_nhl_sd_raw = _prep(_nhl_raw)["home_margin"].std(ddof=1)
lit_nhl_mde = 2.8 * pick(twfe_all, sport="nhl", outcome="home_margin", sample="pooled")["se"]

lit_nfl_margin_over_hfa = (pick(twfe_all, sport="nfl", outcome="home_margin", sample="pooled")["coef"]
                            / pick(noise, sport="nfl", outcome="home_margin")["hfa"])
lit_nfl_win_over_hfa = (pick(twfe_all, sport="nfl", outcome="home_win", sample="pooled")["coef"]
                         / pick(noise, sport="nfl", outcome="home_win")["hfa"])
```

@plosone_nhl_penalties is the closest published work to our NHL result and could be read as
"fan absence removes NHL home advantage". Read precisely, it measures something narrower. Across
three independent samples (NHL playoffs 2015–2020, NHL regular season 2019–2021, and CHL regular
season 2019–2021), away teams received significantly more penalties than home teams **when crowds
were present**, and no significant difference appeared when crowds were absent, with the Home × Crowd
interaction significant in all three (b = .186, p = .024; b = .101, p = .010; b = .095, p = .018).
The paper analyzes **penalty calls only**. It does not analyze goals, margins or wins, and it makes
no claim that the penalty differential translated into home victories.

The two results are therefore compatible, at the level each study measures. Their finding is at
the *mechanism* level; ours is at the *outcome* level. A referee-bias channel can switch off
without moving win probability detectably, for two reasons that both apply here. The channel is
small relative to outcome noise: NHL home advantage in our data is `{python} num(lit_nhl_hfa, 3)` goals per game against a
per-game margin standard deviation of `{python} num(lit_nhl_sd_raw, 2)` goals, and our NHL margin MDE per unit of crowd dose of `{python} num(lit_nhl_mde, 3)` goals exceeds
the entire home advantage. And penalties are one channel among several; travel, familiarity, last
line change and rest are not crowd channels: they do not depend on who is in the arena.

To state it as precisely as we can: *our NHL outcome result is consistent with Guérette et al.
(2021) at the level each study measures. Their mechanism finding stands, and we do not test it.*

The same distinction cuts the other way in basketball, which is why we do not present referee bias
as the established explanation: @gong2022nbafouls finds *no* crowd effect on NBA referee home bias,
while @ganz2024nbafans finds a large crowd effect on NBA outcomes. Mechanism findings and outcome
findings need not track each other.

## What this comparison does and does not license

It does **not** license "our data contradict the published literature". They do not; our NBA
interval reaches the one published estimate we can map into our units, at its upper edge.

It does **not** license any statement of the form "the pooled interval rules out effects larger
than X", for the reasons in @sec-pool.

It does **not** license reading low cross-league heterogeneity as evidence of a common effect. At
$k = `{python} len(SPORTS)`$ the heterogeneity test has no power, and @sec-mlb gives substantive reasons to expect the
true effects to *differ* by league.

And no league's estimate should be described as a clean null. Each is **underpowered, and none is
distinguishable from zero, which is a different thing**: the NFL's point estimate is comparable to
its entire home advantage, at `{python} pct(lit_nfl_margin_over_hfa, 0)` of it on margin and
`{python} pct(lit_nfl_win_over_hfa, 0)` on win probability, per unit of crowd dose.

# Limitations {#sec-limits}

```{python}
#| label: limits-vars
#| include: false
# count regular-season games only -- flagged playoff games are excluded as playoffs anyway.
_nhl_reg = _nhl_raw[~_nhl_raw["is_playoff"].fillna(False)]
_nyi_relocated = _nhl_reg[(_nhl_reg["home_team"] == "NYI") & _nhl_reg["season"].isin([2019, 2020, 2021])
                          & _nhl_reg["relocated_home"].fillna(False) & ~_nhl_reg["is_bubble"].fillna(False)]
lim_nyi_relocated_n = len(_nyi_relocated)
lim_nyi_relocated_pct = lim_nyi_relocated_n / len(_nhl_reg)
assert set(_nyi_relocated["season"]) == {2019, 2020}, "NYI relocated flag now fires outside the two split seasons; reword sec-limits"
# ESPN labels the Islanders' 2020-21 regular-season home games Barclays Center; every one was played at
# Nassau Coliseum (NHL.com, 2020-09-30), so they carry Barclays' empirical capacity, not Nassau's.
_nyi21 = _nhl_raw[(_nhl_raw["home_team"] == "NYI") & (_nhl_raw["season"] == 2021)]
_nyi21_bk = _nyi21[(_nyi21["venue"] == "Barclays Center") & ~_nyi21["is_playoff"].fillna(False)]
lim_nyi21_mislabeled_n = len(_nyi21_bk)
lim_nyi21_cap_ratio = _nyi21.loc[_nyi21["venue"].str.startswith("Nassau"), "capacity"].max() / _nyi21_bk["capacity"].max()
lim_nyi21_dose_mean = _nyi21_bk["crowd_pct"].mean()

# Data-imperfection residual, restated after the 2026-09-16 reopening fix:
# zeros still kept real inside a treated season but dated after the home team's own first
# non-zero game that season. Post-fix, every one of these is a *sourced* re-closure (config
# `reclosures`), not an unverified ambiguity -- check that live rather than asserting it away.
from src.models.twfe import _exclusion_mask
lim_zero_late = 0
lim_zero_late_covered = 0
for _s in SPORTS:
    _p = pd.read_parquet(ROOT / "data" / "processed" / f"{_s}.parquet")
    _p = _p[_p["season"].isin(TREATED[_s]) & ~_exclusion_mask(_p)]
    _first_fans = _p[_p["attendance"] > 0].groupby(["season", "home_team"])["date"].min()
    _z = _p[(_p["attendance"] == 0) & _p["crowd_pct"].notna()]
    _z_first = pd.Series(list(zip(_z["season"], _z["home_team"])), index=_z.index).map(_first_fans)
    _late = _z[_z["date"] > _z_first]
    lim_zero_late += len(_late)
    _late_day = pd.to_datetime(_late["date"]).dt.normalize()
    for _idx, _row in _late.iterrows():
        _day = _late_day.loc[_idx]
        lim_zero_late_covered += int(any(
            rc["team"] == _row["home_team"] and pd.Timestamp(rc["start"]) <= _day <= pd.Timestamp(rc["end"])
            for rc in _sports_cfg[_s]["reclosures"]))
assert lim_zero_late_covered == lim_zero_late, \
    "residual late-zero games are no longer all inside a sourced re-closure; reword the Limitations paragraph"
```

**The identifying assumption is not testable here.** Our coefficient is the crowd effect plus any
other 2020–21 league-wide home-specific shift, and no within-model separation exists
(@sec-assumption). We investigated the bubbles as a way to break the two apart, and @sec-bubble
reports why they do not.

**The design has `{python} words(intro_n_seasons)` season-level assignments and a randomization-inference p-value floor of
`{python} num(res_ri_floor_min, 3)`** (@sec-ri). Nothing in the panel can change that, and @sec-floor shows that adding seasons
would not make it decisive.

**The treatment is measured, not assigned.** The design specifies policy capacity caps; the code
measures realized attendance over empirical capacity. These coincide where caps bind and diverge
where they do not, which is what produces the MLB overlap problem of @sec-mlb. A study built
directly on published per-venue policy caps would identify a cleaner treatment; we did not have
one at per-game resolution across `{python} words(len(SPORTS))` leagues.

**Capacity is empirical, so a normal season is not dose 1.0**, and per-unit coefficients therefore
extrapolate beyond support (about `{python} times(res_mlb_extrapolation, 1)` for MLB's headline, whose normal-season dose averages well
below one). Separately, because 2021 NHL dose never reaches half of capacity, the NHL within-season
regression extrapolates about `{python} times(rob_within_nhl_extrap, 1)` (@sec-nhl). Every ratio in this paper names its scaling
basis for this reason.

**Five known data imperfections are documented and not fixed.** The New York Islanders split home
games between two arenas in 2018–19 and 2019–20, so `{python} thou(lim_nyi_relocated_n)` regular-season games are flagged as relocated and excluded.
This is a false positive against the flag's intent, retained because it is `{python} pct(lim_nyi_relocated_pct, 1)` of regular-season games and the exclusion
is conservative. In 2020–21 the Islanders played every home game at Nassau Coliseum, but ESPN labels
their `{python} thou(lim_nyi21_mislabeled_n)` regular-season home games Barclays Center, so those games take Barclays' empirical
capacity rather than Nassau's and their crowd dose is recorded at about
`{python} num(lim_nyi21_cap_ratio, 2)` of its true value, for one team in one treated season at a mean dose of `{python} num(lim_nyi21_dose_mean, 2)`. Three NHL outdoor games carry a null venue in the source data; all three are
neutral-site and excluded, so no estimate is affected. Finally, the reopening rule of @sec-data still
leaves two residuals we could not close: Detroit's first-fans date is kept at its more heavily
sourced 2021-03-10 game over a single fan account describing earlier January attendance, a judgment
call rather than a settled fact (@sec-zero); and a game where ESPN reports a wrong *non-zero*
attendance count for a team that had not actually reopened would set that team's first-fans date too
early, which we did not check exhaustively against a source. Neither residual includes the
`{python} lim_zero_late` modeled games that still report zero attendance after their home team's own
first non-zero game that season. Every one of those falls inside a sourced re-closure (@sec-data)
and is confirmed real.

**Attendance is announced, not turnstile.** This is a property of ESPN's data and of the other
public sources we checked, and the empirical-capacity denominator is a response to it rather than a solution.

**The study was not pre-registered** (@sec-intro). The specification was changed once, after its
first real-data run, and has not been re-specified since. The main post-hoc additions
belong to one of three declared classes: outcome-blind by construction (the dose-overlap analysis
reads only crowd dose and season), exhaustive and mechanical (leave-one-season-out), or against our
own interest (the noise-floor decomposition, which makes our inference worse). The NHL trend,
season-fixed-effects and within-season diagnostics (@sec-nhl) were added during review rather than
pre-committed, and are reported whichever way they came out. The zero-attendance correction of
@sec-data is outcome-blind in how it was found (an audit of attendance counts) and in its rule
(game dates against documented restriction windows), with one qualification: one MLB-only
diagnostic fit (both outcomes) was seen before the rule was written. One declared exception remains. The
reopening-zeros data correction of @sec-data is not outcome-blind; @sec-zero reports its
largest shift and `reopen_zero_sensitivity.csv` holds every cell both ways. This discipline is not a public
timestamp, and we do not present it as one.

# Conclusion

```{python}
#| label: concl-vars
#| include: false
concl_winprob = {s: pick(twfe_all, sport=s, outcome="home_win", sample="pooled")["coef"] for s in SPORTS}
concl_margin = {"nfl": desc_nfl_margin_pooled, "nba": desc_nba_margin_pooled,
                "nhl": desc_nhl_margin_pooled, "mlb": desc_mlb_margin_pooled}
concl_winpct_pp = {s: pick(desc, sport=s, season="pooled_fullcrowd")["home_win_pct"] * 100 - 50 for s in SPORTS}
concl_n_hfa_games = int(desc[desc["season"] == "pooled_fullcrowd"]["n_games"].sum())
concl_mlb_margin_se = pick(desc, sport="mlb", season="pooled_fullcrowd")["home_margin_se"]
assert abs(concl_margin["mlb"]) < concl_mlb_margin_se, "MLB margin no longer within one SE of zero; reword the conclusion"
# genuine between-season variation is measurable (uncensored) only in the NFL and NBA, every cell.
_cens = noise.assign(c=noise["sd_true_censored"].astype(bool))
assert set(_cens.loc[~_cens["c"], "sport"]) == {"nfl", "nba"} and set(_cens.loc[_cens["c"], "sport"]) == {"mlb", "nhl"}, \
    "sd_true censoring pattern changed; reword the conclusion's NFL/NBA clause"
concl_nfl_win_no2018 = pick(loso, sport="nfl", outcome="home_win", dropped_season=2018)["coef"]
concl_n_games = sum(len(pd.read_parquet(ROOT / "data" / "processed" / f"{s}.parquet", columns=["sport"]))
                     for s in SPORTS)
```

Home-field advantage in the full-crowd regular seasons of 2018–2023 (`{python} thou(concl_n_hfa_games)` games of a `{python} thou(concl_n_games)`-game panel) is `{python} sgn(concl_winpct_pp["nfl"], 1)` percentage points
of win probability in the NFL, `{python} sgn(concl_winpct_pp["nba"], 1)` in the NBA, `{python} sgn(concl_winpct_pp["nhl"], 1)` in the NHL and `{python} sgn(concl_winpct_pp["mlb"], 1)` in MLB, corresponding to
`{python} sgn(concl_margin["nfl"], 2)` points, `{python} sgn(concl_margin["nba"], 2)` points, `{python} sgn(concl_margin["nhl"], 2)` goals and `{python} sgn(concl_margin["mlb"], 2)` runs of scoring margin (MLB's within one standard error of zero).

The crowd-attributable slice of that advantage, estimated off the 2020–21 attendance
restrictions, comes back at `{python} sgn(concl_winprob["nfl"], 3)` (NFL), `{python} sgn(concl_winprob["nba"], 3)` (NBA), `{python} sgn(concl_winprob["nhl"], 3)` (NHL) and `{python} sgn(concl_winprob["mlb"], 3)` (MLB) per unit of
crowd dose on the win-probability scale, with every interval crossing zero, and with two co-primary estimators
(adjusted dose-response and raw comparative interrupted time series) agreeing in sign on
`{python} words(res_coh_sign_agree)` of eight cells and, once the dose-response estimate is scaled by each
league's dose gap, differing in magnitude by `{python} pct(res_coh_gap_min, 1)` to `{python} pct(res_coh_gap_max, 0)` on those (@sec-results).

**We do not conclude that crowds do not matter.** We conclude something narrower and, we think,
more useful:

> In all `{python} words(intro_mde_gt1_count)` league × outcome cells, the effect this design could detect at 80% power is
> larger than the entire home-field advantage of that league, the smallest (`{python} intro_min_ratio_label`) by
> `{python} pct(intro_mde_min_ratio - 1, 0)`.
> (That ratio is per unit of crowd dose; rescaled to each league's normal-season dose, three cells
> fall to approximately one or below.) `{python} words(len(SPORTS)).capitalize()` estimates, each individually underpowered and none
> distinguishable from zero, which is not the same as near zero: the NFL's is nearly its whole home
> advantage per unit of crowd dose (`{python} pct(lit_nfl_win_over_hfa, 0)` on win probability), and falls to
> `{python} sgn(concl_nfl_win_no2018, 3)` without its 2018 season (@sec-loso). In
> the one league where a published estimate can be mapped into our units, it sits at the upper
> edge of our interval. A shared, unmeasured 2020–21 home-specific confound remains, and pooling does not reduce it. The
> claim this study can defend is that it **cannot distinguish zero from a crowd effect accounting
> for all of home-field advantage** under randomization inference, where no p-value this design can produce falls below
> `{python} dot(res_ri_floor_min)`. The team-clustered intervals do exclude a full-advantage effect in
> `{python} words(intro_excl_count)` cells (`{python} intro_excl_cells_str`). The NBA's does not hold against the
> season-level noise floor (@sec-floor); MLB win probability is the one cell where the data lean against a
> crowd effect that large, on an assumption that baseball's 2020 rule changes make least safe (@sec-mlb).

The NHL adds one supporting illustration rather than a finding of its own: within 2021, raw means
favor games with fans while the team-fixed-effects dose coefficient points the other way
(@sec-nhl). One league, on a fit confounded with calendar time, does not establish a general
pattern, and MLB shows no comparable reversal. The NHL illustration is consistent, though, with the between-season
design we adopted, and paid for in power.

Two further findings are, we would argue, the paper's more durable contributions.

**Ordinary season-to-season variation in home advantage exceeds the pandemic signal.** In every
cell at least one ordinary season deviates further from trend than the restricted season does,
though genuine between-season variation, as distinct from sampling noise, is measurable only in the
NFL and NBA (@tbl-floor). In NFL home margin it is `{python} num(res_noise_nfl_sd_true, 2)` points against a total home advantage of `{python} num(res_noise_nfl_hfa, 2)`;
the NFL's 2018 season deviates further from trend, in the opposite direction, than its restricted
2020 season does. Any future study identifying a crowd effect off a single season-level
shock inherits this problem, and should confront it before reporting a clustered p-value over
game-level observations.

**More seasons would not have fixed this.** The two binding variance components (the treated
season's own sampling error and real between-season variation in home advantage) do not shrink as
control seasons are added. On that season-level basis, not per unit of crowd dose, the smallest
detectable effect exceeds the entire home advantage in `{python} words(intro_floor_count)` of eight cells (@sec-floor).
The constraint is not sample size; the pandemic happened once.
